Yan Guo Address: Brown University Email address: guoy@cfm.brown.edu , Alexandru D. Ionescu Address: Princeton University Email address: aionescu@math.princeton.edu and Benoit Pausader Address: LAGA, Université Paris 13 (UMR 7539) Email address: pausader@math.univ-paris13.fr
Abstract.

The fundamental “two-fluid” model for describing plasma dynamics is given by the Euler–Maxwell system, in which compressible ion and electron fluids interact with their own self-consistent electromagnetic field. We prove global stability of a constant neutral background, in the sense that irrotational, smooth and localized perturbations of a constant background with small amplitude lead to global smooth solutions in three space dimensions for the Euler-Maxwell system. Our construction applies equally well to other plasma models such as the Euler-Poisson system for two-fluids and a relativistic Euler-Maxwell system for two fluids. Our solutions appear to be the first nontrivial global smooth solutions in all of these models.

1. Introduction

1.1. Statement of the main result

A plasma is a collection of fast-moving charged particles. It is believed that more than 90% of the matter in the universe is in the form of plasma, from sparse intergalactic plasma, to the interior of stars to neon signs. In addition, understanding of the instability formation in plasma is one of the main challenges for nuclear fusion, in which charged particles are accelerated at high speed to create energy. We refer to [2, 4, 8, 43, 44] for physics references in book form.

At high temperature and velocity, ions and electrons in a plasma tend to become two separate fluids due to their different physical properties (inertia, charge). One of the basic fluid models for describing plasma dynamics is the so-called “two-fluid” model, in which two compressible ion and electron fluids interact with their own self-consistent electromagnetic field. Such an Euler-Maxwell system describes the dynamical evolution of the functions ne,ni:ℝ3→ℝn_{e},n_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, ve,vi,E,B:ℝ3→ℝ3v_{e},v_{i},E,B:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}, which evolve according to the quasi-linear coupled system,

∂tne+div​(ne​ve)=0,ne​me​[∂tve+ve⋅∇ve]+∇pe=−ne​e​[E+vec×B],∂tni+div​(ni​vi)=0,ni​Mi​[∂tvi+vi⋅∇vi]+∇pi=Z​ni​e​[E+vic×B],∂tB+c∇×E=0,∂tE−c∇×B=4πe[neve−Znivi],\begin{split}&\partial_{t}n_{e}+\hbox{div}(n_{e}v_{e})=0,\\ &n_{e}m_{e}\left[\partial_{t}v_{e}+v_{e}\cdot\nabla v_{e}\right]+\nabla p_{e}=-n_{e}e\left[E+\frac{v_{e}}{c}\times B\right],\\ &\partial_{t}n_{i}+\hbox{div}(n_{i}v_{i})=0,\\ &n_{i}M_{i}\left[\partial_{t}v_{i}+v_{i}\cdot\nabla v_{i}\right]+\nabla p_{i}=Zn_{i}e\left[E+\frac{v_{i}}{c}\times B\right],\\ &\partial_{t}B+c\nabla\times E=0,\\ &\partial_{t}E-c\nabla\times B=4\pi e\left[n_{e}v_{e}-Zn_{i}v_{i}\right],\end{split} (1.1)

together with the elliptic equations

div​(B)=0,div​(E)=4​π​e​(Z​ni−ne)\hbox{div}(B)=0,\quad\hbox{div}(E)=4\pi e(Zn_{i}-n_{e}) (1.2)

and two equations of state expressing pep_{e} and pip_{i} in terms of nen_{e} and nin_{i}. These equations describe a plasma composed of electrons and one species of ions. The electrons have charge −e-e, density nen_{e}, mass mem_{e}, velocity vev_{e}, and pressure pep_{e}, and the ions have charge Z​eZe, density nin_{i}, mass MiM_{i}, velocity viv_{i}, and pressure pip_{i}. In addition, cc denotes the speed of light and EE and BB denote the electric and magnetic field. The two equations (1.2) are propagated by the dynamic flow, provided that we assume that they are satisfied at the initial time.

The full Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) with constraint (1.2) forms the foundation of the “two-fluid” model in the plasma theory, which captures the complex dynamics of a plasma due to electromagnetic interactions present in the model. Even at the linear level, there are new ion-acoustic waves, Langmuir waves, as well as light waves etc. At the nonlinear level, the Euler-Maxwell system is the origin of many well-known dispersive PDE, such as KdV [24], KP [36, 39], Zakharov [45], Zakharov-Kuznetsov [36, 39] and NLS, which can be derived from (1.1) and (1.2) via different scaling and asymptotic expansions. We also refer to [3, 11, 12] for derivation of the cold-ion and quasi-neutral equations.

From a PDE viewpoint, the full Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) with constraint (1.2) can be classified as a system of nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with no dissipation and no relaxation effects11 1 When dissipation or relaxation is present, one expects stronger decay, even at the level of the L2L^{2}-norm, see e.g. [38] and the references therein. In our case however, the evolution is time-reversible and we need a different mechanism of decay based on dispersion.. Despite major advances in the mathematical study of hyperbolic conservation laws in one space dimension over the years, no general mathematical theory exists for the construction of global solutions in higher space dimension. One of the reasons is that, for these equations, shock waves (i.e., discontinuities) will generically develop even from smooth initial data (see e.g. John [32]). Even worse, a classical result of Sideris [42] demonstrates that, for the compressible Euler equation for a neutral gas, shock waves will develop even for smooth irrotational initial data with small amplitude. This shock formation was recently further described in [6, 7] (see also [1]).

In this paper we consider perturbations of the flat neutral equilibrium, namely (ne0,ve0,ni0,vi0,E0,B0)=(Z​n0,0,n0,0,0,0)(n_{e}^{0},v_{e}^{0},n_{i}^{0},v_{i}^{0},E^{0},B^{0})=(Zn_{0},0,n_{0},0,0,0), for constant n0>0n_{0}>0 to the Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) and (1.2). In order to state our main result, we normalize the Euler-Maxwell system in the following way. Assume the pressures are given by the formulas22 2 In fact, our approach allows to treat any sufficiently smooth barotropic pressure law, in particular the typical power law pe∼neγep_{e}\sim n_{e}^{\gamma_{e}} for some γe>0\gamma_{e}>0 and similarly for pip_{i}. We refer to Appendix D for more precise statements. Our main theorem is as follows:

Theorem 1.1.

Assume (1.9). Let N0=104N_{0}=10^{4} and assume that

‖(n0,v0,ρ0,u0,E~0,B~0)‖HN0+‖(n0,v0,ρ0,u0,E~0,B~0)‖Z=δ0≤δ¯,div(E~0)+n0−ρ0=0,B~0=ε∇×v0=−∇×u0,\begin{split}&\|(n^{0},v^{0},\rho^{0},u^{0},\tilde{E}^{0},\tilde{B}^{0})\|_{H^{N_{0}}}+\|(n^{0},v^{0},\rho^{0},u^{0},\tilde{E}^{0},\tilde{B}^{0})\|_{Z}=\delta_{0}\leq\overline{\delta},\\ &\hbox{div}(\tilde{E}^{0})+n^{0}-\rho^{0}=0,\qquad\tilde{B}^{0}=\varepsilon\nabla\times v^{0}=-\nabla\times u^{0},\end{split} (1.11)

where δ¯=δ¯​(Cb,T,ε)>0\overline{\delta}=\overline{\delta}(C_{b},T,\varepsilon)>0 is sufficiently small, and the ZZ norm is defined in Definition 4.1. Then there exists a unique global solution (n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)∈C⁡([0,∞):HN0)(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\in C([0,\infty):{H^{N_{0}}}) of the system (1.8) with initial data (n⁡(0),v⁡(0),ρ⁡(0),u⁡(0),E~​(0),B~​(0))=(n0,v0,ρ0,u0,E~0,B~0)(n(0),v(0),\rho(0),u(0),\tilde{E}(0),\tilde{B}(0))=(n^{0},v^{0},\rho^{0},u^{0},\tilde{E}^{0},\tilde{B}^{0}). Moreover, for any t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty),

div(E~)(t)+n(t)−ρ(t)=0,B~(t)=ε∇×v(t)=−∇×u(t), (generalized irrotationality) \hbox{div}(\tilde{E})(t)+n(t)-\rho(t)=0,\qquad\tilde{B}(t)=\varepsilon\nabla\times v(t)=-\nabla\times u(t),\text{ \ (generalized irrotationality) } (1.12)

and, with β:=1/100\beta:=1/100,

‖(n⁡(t),v⁡(t),ρ⁡(t),u⁡(t),E~​(t),B~​(t))‖HN0+sup|α|≤4(1+t)1+β/2∥(Dxαn(t),Dxαv(t),Dxαρ(t),Dxαu(t),DxαE~(t),DxαB~(t)∥L∞≲δ0.\begin{split}&\|(n(t),v(t),\rho(t),u(t),\tilde{E}(t),\tilde{B}(t))\|_{H^{N_{0}}}\\ &+\sup_{|\alpha|\leq 4}(1+t)^{1+\beta/2}\|(D_{x}^{\alpha}n(t),D_{x}^{\alpha}v(t),D_{x}^{\alpha}\rho(t),D_{x}^{\alpha}u(t),D_{x}^{\alpha}\tilde{E}(t),D_{x}^{\alpha}\tilde{B}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\delta_{0}.\end{split} (1.13)

Our main result demonstrates that even though the Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) and (1.2) is much more complicated than the pure Euler system for a neutral gas, it is in fact more stable in the sense that global smooth solutions can persist globally without any shock formations. This is a stark and surprising contrast to Sideris’s result for the pure Euler equations [42].

Remark 1.2.

We make a few remarks about the assumptions in Theorem 1.1.

  • •

    Condition (1.9) is needed for our careful analysis of the dispersion relations that appear in the study of the linearized system (see Lemma A.4 in Appendix A). It is consistent with the relevant physical ranges of the parameters.

  • •

    Our hypothesis imply in particular that the perturbation is electrically neutral, i.e.

    ∫ℝ3[Z​n0​(1+ρ0​(x))−n0​(1+n0​(x))]​𝑑x=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left[Zn_{0}(1+\rho^{0}(x))-n_{0}(1+n^{0}(x))\right]dx=0.

    This is however forced by Maxwell’s relation (1.2) if we assume that the electric perturbation is integrable.

  • •

    The smallness assumption is needed: large deviations from an equilibrium do create shocks [25].

1.2. Important simplified models

The result of blow-up of Sideris for the pure compressible Euler equations [42] can be understood from the fact that small and irrotational perturbations of a constant background for the pure compressible Euler equations obey a quasilinear wave equation without null-structure of the form

(∂t​t−Δ)α=𝒬(α,∇α,∇2α)\left(\partial_{tt}-\Delta\right)\alpha=\mathcal{Q}(\alpha,\nabla\alpha,\nabla^{2}\alpha) (1.14)

where α\alpha is related to the unknown and the right-hand side denotes a quadratic nonlinearity in up to two derivatives of α\alpha. This type of equation has slow decay of linear waves (decay like 1/t1/t) and strong resonances and therefore blow-up or formation of shocks is expected.

The Euler-Maxwell system (1.8) contains a nonlinearity 𝒬\mathcal{Q} essentially similar to the pure compressible Euler case. However, due to self-consistent electromagnetic interaction, the linearized Euler-Maxwell system exhibits much more complex and subtle linear and bilinear dispersive effects than that from the wave equation. The main task in the present work is to systematically track down and exploit such dispersive effects mathematically to preserve smoothness globally in time and prevent shock formation.

In order to put our result in the right context as well as to understand the wealth of dynamics involved in small perturbations of (1.1)-(1.2), we need to introduce some intermediate models. The Euler-Maxwell system (1.1) and (1.2) is such a ‘‘master equations’’ describing very rich and complex plasma dynamics, that it contains several well-known simplified models in plasma physics. For instance, in all physical situations44 4 Indeed, the ratio me/Mim_{e}/M_{i} is no bigger than the ratio of the electron mass to the proton mass which equals 1/18361/1836., me≪Mim_{e}\ll M_{i}. It is then natural to formally set ε=0\varepsilon=0 in (1.8), which leads to simplified one fluid models for either ions (Mi=1M_{i}=1, me=0m_{e}=0) or electrons (Mi=∞M_{i}=\infty, me=1m_{e}=1). Moreover, if all the velocities are much smaller than the speed of light, then Cb≫1C_{b}\gg 1. Formally setting55 5 This is called the electrostatic approximation. Cb=∞C_{b}=\infty and B≡0B\equiv 0 replaces the Maxwell equations by the much simpler Poisson equation. We refer to [3, 11] for other examples.

In the following, we will consider the simplified models in a form which is consistent with the reformulation (1.8) given appropriate approximations. This might look somewhat different from the classical form of these models. However, after an appropriate rescaling the equations should be the same up to cubic and higher-order terms which can be ignored in our situation (see Appendix D).

1.2.1. Single-fluid models

The simplest model we can derive is the Euler-Poisson model for the electrons

∂tn+div​((1+n)​v)=0,∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇n=∇ϕ,Δ​ϕ=n.\begin{split}\partial_{t}n+\hbox{div}((1+n)v)&=0,\\ \partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla n&=\nabla\phi,\\ \Delta\phi&=n.\end{split} (1.15)

Here the magnetic field vanishes B≡0B\equiv 0, and the ions are treated as motionless with a constant density and only form a fixed charged background. Such a simplified system is used for describing Langmuir waves in the two-fluid theory. After suitable change of unknown, (1.15) can be reformulated as

(∂t​t−Δ+1)α=𝒬(α,∇α,∇2α).\left(\partial_{tt}-\Delta+1\right)\alpha=\mathcal{Q}(\alpha,\nabla\alpha,\nabla^{2}\alpha). (1.16)

The linearized Euler-Poisson system for irrotational flows is no longer the acoustic (wave) equation as in the pure Euler system (1.14), but the Klein-Gordon system with “mass term” created by the plasma frequency due to to the electrostatic interaction. Taking advantage of the much better properties of Klein-Gordon equations (faster time decay of linear waves like t−3/2t^{-3/2}, absence of quadratic resonances), global smooth irrotational flows were constructed in [22] via the normal form method of Shatah [41]:

Theorem 1.3 (Stability of a neutral equilibrium [22]).

Solutions of (1.15) with initial data (n0,v0)(n^{0},v^{0}) small, smooth, neutral and irrotational in the sense that

∫ℝ3n0​(x)​𝑑x=0,∇×v0≡0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}n^{0}(x)dx=0,\qquad\nabla\times v^{0}\equiv 0

remain globally smooth and decay to 00 in L∞L^{\infty} as t→+∞t\to+\infty.

The neutral assumption was later removed in [15] and this result was extended to two spatial dimensions independently in [28, 37] (see also [30, 31]). Theorem 1.3 was the first positive result indicating that the dispersive effect alone in the two-fluid theory may prevent shock formation66 6 Another way to prevent shock formation is to introduce exponential damping of the perturbation via dissipation or relaxation (see e.g. [38]). We will not discuss this at all in this paper. and it started an investigation to understand to which extent the introduction of electromagnetic forces could stabilize the full Euler-Maxwell system.

Recently, further progress was made in this direction in the study of another simplified model: the Euler-Poisson equation for the ions77 7 In many works (including [23] and [12, 24, 36]), the the Poisson relation in (1.17) is replaced by −Δ​ϕ=1+ρ−eϕ,-\Delta\phi=1+\rho-e^{\phi}, but, for small perturbations, this agrees with (1.17) up to nonlinear corrections which can be easily handled.:

∂tρ+div​((1+ρ)​u)=0,∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇ρ=−∇ϕ,−Δ​ϕ=ρ−ϕ.\begin{split}\partial_{t}\rho+\hbox{div}((1+\rho)u)&=0,\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\rho&=-\nabla\phi,\\ -\Delta\phi&=\rho-\phi.\end{split} (1.17)

Here the electron dynamics with constant temperature is decoupled from the ion dynamics via the Boltzmann relation. The model equation then becomes

(∂t​t−Δ+(−Δ)(1−Δ)−1)α=|∇|𝒬(α,∇α)\left(\partial_{tt}-\Delta+(-\Delta)(1-\Delta)^{-1}\right)\alpha=|\nabla|\mathcal{Q}(\alpha,\nabla\alpha) (1.18)

This system has intermediate behavior between (1.14) and (1.16). The linearized solutions decay slowly (like t−4/3t^{-4/3}) and create many strong degeneracies near the zero frequency, where the dispersion relation is similar to the wave dispersion up to third order (see λi\lambda_{i} in Lemma A.4). Nevertheless, the first and third authors were able to obtain an analogue of Theorem 1.3 for perturbations of a neutral equilibrium by using a variation on the normal form method, controlling bilinear multipliers with rough coefficients using arguments inspired by [26]. Here, a crucial property is the fact that the nonlinearity is an exact derivative, which helps compensate for the degeneracy at the 00 frequency.

1.2.2. Two-fluid models with different speeds

Both systems (1.15) and (1.17) can be reduced (under the irrotational assumption) to a (complex) scalar quasilinear equation with one speed. This is no longer the case for more complicated two-fluid models which yield quasilinear system with different speeds. Bilinear interactions in quasilinear systems generically create resonant sets of 2D spheres in the phase space, which are very challenging to control analytically. This was first studied in [13] for the case of semilinear systems of Klein-Gordon equations with different speeds (see also [10] for a study of a system with different masses) and led in [14] to the first construction of global smooth solutions for the Euler-Maxwell equation for electrons,

∂tn+div​((1+n)​v)=0,∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇n=−[E+v×B],∂tB+∇×E=0,∂tE−C∇×B=(1+n)​v\begin{split}\partial_{t}n+\hbox{div}((1+n)v)&=0,\\ \partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla n&=-\left[E+v\times B\right],\\ \partial_{t}B+\nabla\times E&=0,\\ \partial_{t}E-C\nabla\times B&=(1+n)v\end{split} (1.19)

with constraints div​(B)=0\hbox{div}(B)=0 and div​(E)=n\hbox{div}(E)=n :

Theorem 1.4 (Stability in the Euler-Maxwell system for electrons [14, 29]).

A solution of (1.19) with initial data (n0,v0,E0,B0)(n^{0},v^{0},E^{0},B^{0}) small, smooth, compactly supported, neutral and irrotational in the sense that

∫ℝ3n0​(x)​dx=0,∫ℝ3B0​(x)​dx=0,∇×v0+C​B0≡0\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}n^{0}(x)dx=0,\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}B^{0}(x)dx=0,\quad\nabla\times v^{0}+CB^{0}\equiv 0\end{split}

remains global and smooth and decays to 00 in L∞L^{\infty}.

This was first shown in [14] under additional generic conditions on the parameters. Later in [29], the generic condition was removed and a stronger (integrable) decay was obtained, providing a robust approach even in the quasilinear case. The model system is

(∂t​t−Δ+1)α=𝒬1​(α,β,∇α,∇β,∇2α,∇2β)(∂t​t−CΔ+1)β=𝒬2​(α,β,∇α,∇β,∇2α,∇2β).\begin{split}\left(\partial_{tt}-\Delta+1\right)\alpha&=\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\alpha,\beta,\nabla\alpha,\nabla\beta,\nabla^{2}\alpha,\nabla^{2}\beta)\\ \left(\partial_{tt}-C\Delta+1\right)\beta&=\mathcal{Q}_{2}(\alpha,\beta,\nabla\alpha,\nabla\beta,\nabla^{2}\alpha,\nabla^{2}\beta).\end{split} (1.20)

It is important to note that the speed of the electron fluids is different from the speed of the magnetic field, so that new analytical tools are needed to estimate the 2D resonant sphere in the phase space. The main result of [29] is the natural analogue of Theorem 1.3 and it is the foundation of the approach we use in this work. Note that in this case, we also need to introduce a decay condition on the initial data in order to be able to perform a more refined analysis of the solutions.

1.3. Description of the Method

We use a combination of dispersive analysis and energy estimate, relying heavily on the Fourier transform (see [5, 16, 17, 26, 34, 35, 41] for previous seminal works). To overcome the quasilinear nature of the nonlinearity and ensure global existence, we use classical high order energy estimates to make up for the loss of derivatives in the nonlinearity. Global existence follows if a certain norm of lower regularity remains bounded and decays faster than 1/t.1/t.

Such a crucial decay property is established by a semilinear analysis of systems of dispersive equations. Expecting some form of scattering, we express the solution as a free evolution88 8 I.e. a solution to the linearized equation. from a profile which varies more slowly in time. After suitable algebraic manipulations, and appropriate use of the Fourier transform, we need to study bilinear operators TT of the form

T⁡[f,g]^​(ξ)=∫ℝ∫ℝ3ei​t​Φ​(ξ,η)​m​(ξ,η)​f^​(ξ−η,t)​g^​(η,t)​𝑑η​𝑑t.\widehat{T[f,g]}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}e^{it\Phi(\xi,\eta)}m(\xi,\eta)\widehat{f}(\xi-\eta,t)\widehat{g}(\eta,t)d\eta dt. (1.21)

with a phase Φ\Phi which is specific to each interaction and which is of the form

Φ⁡(ξ,η)=Λ0​(ξ)±Λ1​(ξ−η)±Λ2​(η),Λj∈{Λi,Λe,Λb},\Phi(\xi,\eta)=\Lambda_{0}(\xi)\pm\Lambda_{1}(\xi-\eta)\pm\Lambda_{2}(\eta),\quad\Lambda_{j}\in\{\Lambda_{i},\Lambda_{e},\Lambda_{b}\}, (1.22)

where the functions Λj\Lambda_{j} are defined from the linearized system and given in (3.12). As a first approximation, one may think of ff, gg as being smooth bump functions and mm being essentially a smooth cut-off, and the main challenge is to estimate efficiently the infinite time integral. It then becomes clear that a key role is played by the properties of the function Φ\Phi and in particular by the points where it is stationary,

∇(t,η)[t​Φ​(ξ,η)]=0,i.e.Φ⁡(ξ,η)=0​ and ​∇ηΦ​(ξ,η)=0.\nabla_{(t,\eta)}[t\Phi(\xi,\eta)]=0,\quad\hbox{i.e.}\quad\Phi(\xi,\eta)=0\hbox{ and }\nabla_{\eta}\Phi(\xi,\eta)=0. (1.23)

The collection of such points form the space-time resonant set. This was already highlighted in [16] and forms the basis of the space-time resonance method. In some situations, one has no or few fully stationary points and the task is mainly to propagate enough smoothness of f^\hat{f}, g^\hat{g} to exploit (non)-stationary phase arguments.

However, as in the case of the Euler-Maxwell equation for electrons (1.19), the space-time resonance set can be a 2D sphere. In addition, the linearized system for the full two fluid model is now coupled, which makes the derivation of the dispersive system in Section 3 more involved and requires a careful study of the dispersion relations Λj\Lambda_{j} appearing in (1.22) (see Lemma A.4). Moreover, the appearance of an “ion-like” dispersion relation Λi\Lambda_{i}, similar to that in (1.17), leads to additional mathematical difficulties of slower time decay of linear solutions, rough bilinear multipliers and rough phase around the zero frequency.

To overcome these new difficulties, we employ and extend the method developed in [28, 29]. We seek an appropriate space BB satisfying two requirements: first, the bilinear operator TT in (1.21) needs to be bounded

T:B×B→B,T:B\times B\rightarrow B, (1.24)

second, the free flow of the linearized Euler-Mawell system (1.8) with initial data bounded in the space BB should belong to a space like Lt1​Lx∞L_{t}^{1}L_{x}^{\infty}, which has sufficiently strong time decay to close the energy estimate.

This strategy, initiated in the previous works [28, 29] shares similarities with the space-time resonance method as developed in [13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19] but with new types of function space localized in both space and frequency, which are naturally compatible with the introduction of fractional powers of the weights (like x−1−ε​L2x^{-1-\varepsilon}L^{2} for the B1B^{1}-norm below), and with new bilinear estimates. We find this approach more precise and flexible analytically, which is crucial to analyze the complicated phase function (1.22) arising in the Euler-Maxwell system. Together with orthogonality arguments and localized decay estimates, this allows to overcome the central difficulty of controlling delicate space-time resonant points in (1.23).

We also mention the works in [9, 40] which consider global existence in dispersive equations or systems with nonlinearity with small power without assuming any weights on the initial data (see also [21] and the references therein). It appears, however that such approach would be very difficult to carry on in the context of a system like (1.1) due to the loss of derivative in the nonlinearity. In addition, even in a purely semilinear setting, the analysis of the most delicate space-time resonances seems presently out of reach when the functions have too rough Fourier transforms.

1.3.1. Choice of the norms

In order to define such a space BB, we measure localization both in space and in frequency. We quantify all these “coordinates” all the way to the uncertainty principle and decompose an arbitrary function as a sum of “atoms”:

f=∑X⋅N≥1QX​PN​f,(QX​f)​(x)≃1X≤|x|≤2​X​(x)​f​(x),(PN​f^)​(ξ)≃1N≤|ξ|≤2​N​(ξ)​f^​(ξ).f=\sum_{X\cdot N\geq 1}Q_{X}P_{N}f,\quad(Q_{X}f)(x)\simeq\mathfrak{1}_{X\leq|x|\leq 2X}(x)f(x),\quad(\widehat{P_{N}f})(\xi)\simeq\mathfrak{1}_{N\leq|\xi|\leq 2N}(\xi)\hat{f}(\xi).

We can then define the norms for the space BB on each atom. The simplest norm giving the appropriate decay would be a weighted space x−1−ε​L2x^{-1-\varepsilon}L^{2} and this is the main motivation for our “strong” norm B1B^{1}. Unfortunately, some interactions seem to produce outputs which are not bounded in this norm around a 2D resonant sphere. To account for this, we also introduce another kind of atoms, the “weak” atoms, bounded only in B2B^{2} which barely fail to be in x−1​L2x^{-1}L^{2}, but are essentially concentrated on the 2​D2D-resonant spheres. Finally, each atom is allowed to be a combination of the two above types:

‖f‖=supX⋅N≥1‖QX​PN​f‖BX,N,‖g‖BX,N=‖g‖BX,N1+BX,N2=infg=g1+g2{‖g1‖BX,N1+‖g2‖BX,N2}.\|f\|=\sup_{X\cdot N\geq 1}\|Q_{X}P_{N}f\|_{B_{X,N}},\qquad\|g\|_{B_{X,N}}=\|g\|_{B_{X,N}^{1}+B_{X,N}^{2}}=\inf_{g=g_{1}+g_{2}}\{\|g_{1}\|_{B_{X,N}^{1}}+\|g_{2}\|_{B_{X,N}^{2}}\}.

We refer to Definition 4.1 for the precise definition of the ZZ norm that we use and to Lemma A.5 in Appendix A for the proof that these norms yield the desired integrability upon application of the linear flow.

1.3.2. Analysis of the bilinear operators

Once the form of the norm has been assessed, the main difficulty is to understand the bilinear interactions in (1.21) and to fine-tune the norms to ensure that they are appropriately bounded as in (1.24). After quantifying all the information, one needs to treat a huge sum of elementary interactions (even for a single atom as an output). However, appropriate use of energy-estimate, simple orthogonality arguments and finite speed of propagation quickly limit the cases to only a few possibilities, see Proposition 5.4 and Lemma 5.5. Then non-stationary phase analysis allows to focus on the space-time resonant sets as in (1.23). This is where the bulk of the work is done, following a previous work [29] where such an analysis was performed on the simplified Euler-Maxwell equation for the electrons.

After a careful analysis of the interactions done in Appendix B, we isolate three different problematic space-time resonant sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

  • •

    Case A: we have the case of a “classical” 2​D2D sphere

    𝒮A={(ξ,η)=(R​ω,r​ω),ω∈𝕊2},R≠0,r≠0\mathcal{S}_{A}=\{(\xi,\eta)=(R\omega,r\omega),\,\,\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}\},\quad R\neq 0,\,\,r\neq 0

    which already appears in the analysis of (1.20) and which is responsible for the introduction of the “weak” atoms. Fortunately, here the phase is nondegenerate and we can perform an efficient stationary phase analysis and use additional refined orthogonality arguments as in [29].

  • •

    Case B: we have a first degenerate sphere

    𝒮B={(ξ,η)=(R′​ω,0),ω∈𝕊2},R′≠0\mathcal{S}_{B}=\{(\xi,\eta)=(R^{\prime}\omega,0),\,\,\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}\},\quad R^{\prime}\neq 0

    where in addition, the phase is not smooth in η\eta.

    In this case, we use the fact that the speed of propagation of the singular perturbation is slower than expected, the fact that the phase is weakly elliptic and a careful adaptation of the refined orthogonality analysis of Case A, keeping track of how the bound deteriorate as η→0\eta\to 0.

  • •

    Case C: the presence of an “ion-like” dispersion relation brings in a strong degenerate set at 00

    𝒮D={(ξ,η)=(0,r′​ω),ω∈𝕊2},r′≠0​ or ​r′=0.\mathcal{S}_{D}=\{(\xi,\eta)=(0,r^{\prime}\omega),\,\,\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}\},\quad r^{\prime}\neq 0\hbox{ or }r^{\prime}=0.

    Here the problem comes from the strong degeneracy of the phase. Similar problems already appeared for the Euler-Poisson equation for the ions (1.17), but for (1.1) we need more refined multiplier estimate and orthogonality arguments, combined with additional finite speed of propagation estimates and use of the null-form structure coming from the presence of a derivative in front of the nonlinearity as in (1.18) in order to overcome the loss coming from the roughness of the multiplier after application of a normal form transformation.

Our approach seems flexible and robust and we illustrate this by extending the main results to other problems of interest with a similar structure in Appendix D, Most notably variants of (1.1) which enjoy natural (Galilean or Lorentz) symmetry.

1.3.3. Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we obtain a classical local well-posedness result in the energy space. In Section 3, we reduce the Euler-Maxwell system (1.8) into a quasilinear dispersive system and identify the linearized system, together with the main structure of the nonlinearity. In Section 4, we introduce the function space ZZ (see 4.5) and prove the main Theorem 1.1 assuming boundedness of the relevant bilinear integral operators as in (1.21)-(1.24). In Section 5, we study the case of nonresonant interactions for localized atoms. Sections 6-7-8 are then devoted to the study of the resonant interactions.

In Section 6, we study Case A resonant interactions. We first make use of an efficient parametrization pσ;μ,νp^{\sigma;\mu,\nu} in (6.5), (6.9)-(6.11), then control precisely the output of interactions of “atoms” by carefully designed Bk,j2B_{k,j}^{2} norm defined in (4.5) as well as additional L2L^{2} orthogonality argument in the spirit of [29].

In Section 7, we study Case B resonant interactions. We make use of a precise analytic characterization of Case B (Lemma 7.2), decay estimates Lemma A.5, as well as an orthogonality argument to control the L2L^{2} norm to complete the analysis.

Section 8 is devoted to the study of Case C. We take advantage of the geometry of angles between η,ξ\eta,\xi and ξ−η\xi-\eta to obtain extra regularity to overcome the singularity near zero frequency.

Finally, in Appendix A, we isolate relevant information on the structure of the dispersion relations λi\lambda_{i}, λe\lambda_{e} and λb\lambda_{b} and provide various stationary-phase estimates that are needed throughout the proof; in Appendix B, we classify the quadratic resonances that may appear; in Appendix C, we provide, for the convenience of the reader the precise form of the 6161 multipliers that appear in the quadratic interactions, and in Appendix D, we extend the results to cover various other systems with a similar structure.

2. Energy estimates and the local existence theory

The local existence theory for (1.8) is based on energy estimates. These in turn are obtained from the physical energy. The (local) energy identity reads

∂t𝔢+div​[𝔍e+𝔍i+𝔍b]=0,𝔢:=T​n22+ε⁡(n+1)​|v|22+ρ22+(ρ+1)​|u|22+|E~|22+Cbε​|B~|22,𝔍e:={Tn+ε|v|22}(n+1)v,𝔍i:={ρ+|u|22}(ρ+1)u,𝔍b:=CbεE~×B~.\begin{split}&\partial_{t}\mathfrak{e}+\hbox{div}\left[\mathfrak{J}_{e}+\mathfrak{J}_{i}+\mathfrak{J}_{b}\right]=0,\\ &\mathfrak{e}:=T\frac{n^{2}}{2}+\varepsilon(n+1)\frac{|v|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\rho^{2}}{2}+(\rho+1)\frac{|u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{|\tilde{E}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{C_{b}}{\varepsilon}\frac{|\tilde{B}|^{2}}{2},\\ &\mathfrak{J}_{e}:=\left\{Tn+\varepsilon\frac{|v|^{2}}{2}\right\}(n+1)v,\quad\mathfrak{J}_{i}:=\left\{\rho+\frac{|u|^{2}}{2}\right\}(\rho+1)u,\quad\mathfrak{J}_{b}:=\frac{C_{b}}{\varepsilon}\tilde{E}\times\tilde{B}.\end{split}

From this, we obtain our higher order energies. For any (n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)∈H~N(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\in\widetilde{H}^{N} we define

ℰN:=∑|γ|≤N∫ℝ3[T​|Dxγ​n|2+ε⁡(1+n)​|Dxγ​v|2+|Dxγ​ρ|2+(ρ+1)​|Dxγ​u|2+|Dxγ​E~|2+Cbε​|Dxγ​B~|2]​𝑑x.\mathcal{E}_{N}:=\sum_{|\gamma|\leq N}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\big[T|D_{x}^{\gamma}n|^{2}+\varepsilon(1+n)|D_{x}^{\gamma}v|^{2}+|D_{x}^{\gamma}\rho|^{2}+(\rho+1)|D_{x}^{\gamma}u|^{2}+|D_{x}^{\gamma}\tilde{E}|^{2}+\frac{C_{b}}{\varepsilon}|D_{x}^{\gamma}\tilde{B}|^{2}\big]\,dx. (2.1)

provided that |ρ|+|ρ′|≤M+1|\rho|+|\rho^{\prime}|\leq M+1, M≥1M\geq 1, and |ρ|,|ρ′|≥1|\rho|,|\rho^{\prime}|\geq 1. Using also the equations we estimate

|IP+∑k=13∫ℝ32TPn⋅(1+n)⋅P∂kvkdx|≲A(t)∥(n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)∥H~N2,|I​IP|≲A⁡(t)​‖(n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)‖H~N2,|I​I​IP+∑j=13∫ℝ3[2​T​P​∂jn⋅(1+n)⋅P​vj+2​P​E~j⋅P​vj⋅(1+n)]​dx|≲A⁡(t)​‖(n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)‖H~N2,\begin{split}&\Big|I_{P}+\sum_{k=1}^{3}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}2TPn\cdot(1+n)\cdot P\partial_{k}v_{k}\,dx\Big|\lesssim A(t)\|(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\|_{\widetilde{H}^{N}}^{2},\\ &\Big|II_{P}\Big|\lesssim A(t)\|(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\|_{\widetilde{H}^{N}}^{2},\\ &\Big|III_{P}+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\big[2TP\partial_{j}n\cdot(1+n)\cdot Pv_{j}+2P\tilde{E}_{j}\cdot Pv_{j}\cdot(1+n)\big]\,dx\Big|\lesssim A(t)\|(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\|_{\widetilde{H}^{N}}^{2},\end{split}

In addition,

Therefore

|dd​t​ℰP′|≲A⁡(t)​‖(n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)‖H~N2,\Big|\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{P}\Big|\lesssim A(t)\|(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\|_{\widetilde{H}^{N}}^{2},

and the bound (2.3) follows since ℰN=∑P=Dxγ,|γ|≤NℰP′≈‖(n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)‖H~N2\mathcal{E}_{N}=\sum_{P=D^{\gamma}_{x},\,|\gamma|\leq N}\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{P}\approx\|(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\|_{\widetilde{H}^{N}}^{2}.

Finally, to verify that the identities (2.5) are propagated by the flow, we let

X:=n−ρ+div(E~),Y:=B~−ε∇×v,Z:=B~+∇×u.X:=n-\rho+\hbox{div}(\tilde{E}),\qquad Y:=\tilde{B}-\varepsilon\nabla\times v,\qquad Z:=\tilde{B}+\nabla\times u.

Using the equations in (1.8) we calculate

∂tX=∂tn−∂tρ+∑j=13∂j∂tE~j=−∑j=13∂j[(1+n)vj−(1+ρ)uj]+∑j=13∂j[(1+n)vj−(1+ρ)uj]=0,\partial_{t}X=\partial_{t}n-\partial_{t}\rho+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{j}\partial_{t}\tilde{E}_{j}=-\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{j}[(1+n)v_{j}-(1+\rho)u_{j}]+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{j}[(1+n)v_{j}-(1+\rho)u_{j}]=0,

∂t(∑k=13∂kB~k)=0,\partial_{t}\big(\sum_{k=1}^{3}\partial_{k}\tilde{B}_{k}\big)=0,

∑k=13∂kB~k≡0,∑k=13∂kYk≡0,∑k=13∂kZk≡0.\sum_{k=1}^{3}\partial_{k}\tilde{B}_{k}\equiv 0,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{3}\partial_{k}Y_{k}\equiv 0,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{3}\partial_{k}Z_{k}\equiv 0.

∂tY=∇×(v×Y),∂tZ=∇×(u×Z).\partial_{t}Y=\nabla\times(v\times Y),\qquad\partial_{t}Z=\nabla\times(u\times Z).

Using energy estimates it follows easily that Y≡0,Z≡0Y\equiv 0,Z\equiv 0, as desired. ∎

3. Derivation of the main dispersive system

The main part of this paper is devoted to obtain global time integrability of the function AA defined in (2.4), so as to be able to propagate energy control using (2.3). In order to do this, one needs to turn the system (1.8)–(1.10) into a quasilinear system of dispersive equations. This is the purpose of this section. The main results are summarized in Proposition 3.2.

For ξ∈ℝ3\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and α=1,2,3\alpha=1,2,3 we define

|∇|(ξ):=|ξ|,Rα(ξ):=iξα/|ξ|,Qα​β(ξ):=i∈α​γ​βξγ/|ξ|,H1(ξ):=1+|ξ|2,Hε(ξ):=ε−1/21+T​|ξ|2,Λb(ξ):=ε−1/21+ε+Cb​|ξ|2.\begin{split}&|\nabla|(\xi):=|\xi|,\qquad R_{\alpha}(\xi):=i\xi_{\alpha}/|\xi|,\qquad Q_{\alpha\beta}(\xi):=i\in_{\alpha\gamma\beta}\xi_{\gamma}/|\xi|,\\ &H_{1}(\xi):=\sqrt{1+|\xi|^{2}},\qquad H_{\varepsilon}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+T|\xi|^{2}},\qquad\Lambda_{b}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+\varepsilon+C_{b}|\xi|^{2}}.\end{split} (3.1)

By a slight abuse of notation we also let |∇|,Rα,Q,H1,Hε,Λb|\nabla|,R_{\alpha},Q,H_{1},H_{\varepsilon},\Lambda_{b} denote the operators on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} defined by the corresponding Fourier multipliers. Notice that

Q3=Q and Q​A=|∇|−1​(∇×A)​ for any vector-field ​A.Q^{3}=Q\qquad\text{ and }\qquad QA=|\nabla|^{-1}(\nabla\times A)\text{ for any vector-field }A.

Closer inspection of the system (1.8)–(1.10) shows a decoupling of the magnetic unknowns curl​(E)\hbox{curl}(E), BB and the electrostatic (Euler-Poisson) unknowns nn, ρ\rho, div​(v)\hbox{div}(v) and div​(u)\hbox{div}(u). More precisely, we may define

2​Ub:=Λb​|∇|−1​Q​B~−i​Q2​E~,h:=−|∇|−1​div​(v),g:=−|∇|−1​div​(u).2U_{b}:=\Lambda_{b}|\nabla|^{-1}Q\tilde{B}-iQ^{2}\tilde{E},\qquad h:=-|\nabla|^{-1}\hbox{div}(v),\qquad g:=-|\nabla|^{-1}\hbox{div}(u).

Recalling that B~=ε∇×v=−∇×u\tilde{B}=\varepsilon\nabla\times v=-\nabla\times u and div​(E~)=ρ−n\hbox{div}(\tilde{E})=\rho-n, the functions Ub,h,gU_{b},h,g together with nn, ρ\rho allow us to recover all the physical unknowns, i.e.

B~=2​Λb−1​|∇|​Q​Re​(Ub),v=∇|∇|−1h+2εΛb−1Re(Ub),u=∇|∇|−1g−2Λb−1Re(Ub),E~=−∇|∇|−2​[ρ−n]−2​Im​(Ub).\begin{split}\tilde{B}&=2\Lambda_{b}^{-1}|\nabla|Q\hbox{Re}(U_{b}),\\ v&=\nabla|\nabla|^{-1}h+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\hbox{Re}(U_{b}),\\ u&=\nabla|\nabla|^{-1}g-2\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\hbox{Re}(U_{b}),\\ \tilde{E}&=-\nabla|\nabla|^{-2}\left[\rho-n\right]-2\hbox{Im}(U_{b}).\end{split} (3.2)

Let

Aα=2​Λb−1​Re​(Ub,α).A_{\alpha}=2\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\hbox{Re}(U_{b,\alpha}).

In terms of n,h,ρ,g,Ubn,h,\rho,g,U_{b} the system (1.8)-(1.10) becomes

∂tn−|∇|​h=−∂α[nRαh]−(1/ε)∂α[nAα],∂tρ−|∇|​g=−∂α[ρRαg]+∂α[ρAα],∂th+|∇|−1​Hε2​n−ε−1​|∇|−1​ρ=−(1/2)​|∇|​[Rα​h​Rα​h]−ε−1|∇|[Rα​h​Aα]−(ε−2/2)​|∇|​[Aα​Aα],∂tg−|∇|−1​n+|∇|−1​H12​ρ=−(1/2)​|∇|​[Rα​g​Rα​g]+|∇|[Rα​g​Aα]−(1/2)​|∇|​[Aα​Aα],∂tUb,α+i​Λb​Ub,α=−(i/2)​Qα​β2​[n​Rβ​h−ρ​Rβ​g+ε−1​n​Aβ+ρ​Aβ],\begin{split}\partial_{t}n-|\nabla|h&=-\partial_{\alpha}\left[nR_{\alpha}h\right]-(1/\varepsilon)\partial_{\alpha}\left[nA_{\alpha}\right],\\ \partial_{t}\rho-|\nabla|g&=-\partial_{\alpha}\left[\rho R_{\alpha}g\right]+\partial_{\alpha}\left[\rho A_{\alpha}\right],\\ \partial_{t}h+|\nabla|^{-1}H_{\varepsilon}^{2}n-\varepsilon^{-1}|\nabla|^{-1}\rho&=-(1/2)|\nabla|\left[R_{\alpha}hR_{\alpha}h\right]-\varepsilon^{-1}|\nabla|\left[R_{\alpha}hA_{\alpha}\right]-(\varepsilon^{-2}/2)|\nabla|\left[A_{\alpha}A_{\alpha}\right],\\ \partial_{t}g-|\nabla|^{-1}n+|\nabla|^{-1}H_{1}^{2}\rho&=-(1/2)|\nabla|\left[R_{\alpha}gR_{\alpha}g\right]+|\nabla|\left[R_{\alpha}gA_{\alpha}\right]-(1/2)|\nabla|\left[A_{\alpha}A_{\alpha}\right],\\ \partial_{t}U_{b,\alpha}+i\Lambda_{b}U_{b,\alpha}&=-(i/2)Q^{2}_{\alpha{\beta}}[nR_{\beta}h-\rho R_{\beta}g+\varepsilon^{-1}nA_{\beta}+\rho A_{\beta}],\end{split} (3.3)

where the left-hand sides of the equations above are linear in the variables n,h,ρ,g,Ubn,h,\rho,g,U_{b}, and the right-hand sides are quadratic.

We make linear changes of variables to diagonalize this system. Let

Λe:=ε−1/2(1+ε)−(T+ε)​Δ+((1−ε)−(T−ε)​Δ)2+4​ε2,Λi:=ε−1/2(1+ε)−(T+ε)​Δ−((1−ε)−(T−ε)​Δ)2+4​ε2,\begin{split}&\Lambda_{e}:=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{\frac{(1+\varepsilon)-(T+\varepsilon)\Delta+\sqrt{\left((1-\varepsilon)-(T-\varepsilon)\Delta\right)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}{2}},\\ &\Lambda_{i}:=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{\frac{(1+\varepsilon)-(T+\varepsilon)\Delta-\sqrt{\left((1-\varepsilon)-(T-\varepsilon)\Delta\right)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}{2}},\end{split} (3.4)

such that

(Λe2−Hε2)​(Hε2−Λi2)=ε−1,Λe2−H12=Hε2−Λi2.(\Lambda_{e}^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}^{2})(H_{\varepsilon}^{2}-\Lambda_{i}^{2})=\varepsilon^{-1},\qquad\Lambda_{e}^{2}-H_{1}^{2}=H_{\varepsilon}^{2}-\Lambda_{i}^{2}. (3.5)

Let

R:=Λe2−Hε2Hε2−Λi2,R:=\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda_{e}^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}^{2}}{H_{\varepsilon}^{2}-\Lambda_{i}^{2}}}, (3.6)

and notice that

Λe2−Hε2=ε−1/2R,Hε2−Λi2=ε−1/2R−1.\Lambda_{e}^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}^{2}=\varepsilon^{-1/2}R,\qquad H_{\varepsilon}^{2}-\Lambda_{i}^{2}=\varepsilon^{-1/2}R^{-1}. (3.7)

Let

Ue:=12​1+R2​[−ε1/2​|∇|−1​Λe​n+R​|∇|−1​Λe​ρ−i​ε1/2​h+i​R​g],Ui:=12​1+R2​[ε1/2​R​|∇|−1​Λi​n+|∇|−1​Λi​ρ+i​ε1/2​R​h+i​g].\begin{split}&U_{e}:=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[-\varepsilon^{1/2}|\nabla|^{-1}\Lambda_{e}n+R|\nabla|^{-1}\Lambda_{e}\rho-i\varepsilon^{1/2}h+iRg\big],\\ &U_{i}:=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[\varepsilon^{1/2}R|\nabla|^{-1}\Lambda_{i}n+|\nabla|^{-1}\Lambda_{i}\rho+i\varepsilon^{1/2}Rh+ig\big].\end{split} (3.8)

Using the system (3.3) it is easy to check that the complex variables UeU_{e}, UiU_{i} and UbU_{b} satisfy the identities

(∂t+iΛe)Ue=𝒩e,(∂t+iΛi)Ui=𝒩i,(∂t+iΛb)Ub,α=𝒩b,α,\begin{split}&(\partial_{t}+i\Lambda_{e})U_{e}=\mathcal{N}_{e},\\ &(\partial_{t}+i\Lambda_{i})U_{i}=\mathcal{N}_{i},\\ &(\partial_{t}+i\Lambda_{b})U_{b,\alpha}=\mathcal{N}_{b,\alpha},\end{split} (3.9)

where

ℜ(𝒩e)=Λe​Rα2​1+R2[ε1/2(nRαh)−R(ρRαg)+ε−1/2(nAα)+R(ρAα)],ℑ(𝒩e)=|∇|4​1+R2[ε−3/2(εRαh+Aα)(εRαh+Aα)−R[(Rαg−Aα)(Rαg−Aα)]],ℜ(𝒩i)=−Λi​Rα2​1+R2[ε1/2R(nRαh)+(ρRαg)+ε−1/2R(nAα)−(ρAα)],ℑ(𝒩i)=−|∇|4​1+R2[ε−3/2R[(εRαh+Aα)(εRαh+Aα)]+(Rαg−Aα)(Rαg−Aα)],ℜ⁡(𝒩b,α)=0,ℑ⁡(𝒩b,α)=−(1/2)​Qα​β2​[n​Rβ​h−ρ​Rβ​g+ε−1​n​Aβ+ρ​Aβ].\begin{split}&\Re(\mathcal{N}_{e})=\frac{\Lambda_{e}R_{\alpha}}{2\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[\varepsilon^{1/2}(nR_{\alpha}h)-R(\rho R_{\alpha}g)+\varepsilon^{-1/2}(nA_{\alpha})+R(\rho A_{\alpha})\big],\\ &\Im(\mathcal{N}_{e})=\frac{|\nabla|}{4\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[\varepsilon^{-3/2}(\varepsilon R_{\alpha}h+A_{\alpha})(\varepsilon R_{\alpha}h+A_{\alpha})-R[(R_{\alpha}g-A_{\alpha})(R_{\alpha}g-A_{\alpha})]\big],\\ &\Re(\mathcal{N}_{i})=\frac{-\Lambda_{i}R_{\alpha}}{2\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[\varepsilon^{1/2}R(nR_{\alpha}h)+(\rho R_{\alpha}g)+\varepsilon^{-1/2}R(nA_{\alpha})-(\rho A_{\alpha})\big],\\ &\Im(\mathcal{N}_{i})=\frac{-|\nabla|}{4\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}\big[\varepsilon^{-3/2}R[(\varepsilon R_{\alpha}h+A_{\alpha})(\varepsilon R_{\alpha}h+A_{\alpha})]+(R_{\alpha}g-A_{\alpha})(R_{\alpha}g-A_{\alpha})\big],\\ &\Re(\mathcal{N}_{b,\alpha})=0,\\ &\Im(\mathcal{N}_{b,\alpha})=-(1/2)Q^{2}_{\alpha\beta}\left[nR_{\beta}h-\rho R_{\beta}g+\varepsilon^{-1}nA_{\beta}+\rho A_{\beta}\right].\end{split} (3.10)

The system (3.9) is our main dispersive system, which is diagonalized at the linear level. To analyze it we have to express the nonlinearities 𝒩e\mathcal{N}_{e}, 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i}, and 𝒩b,α\mathcal{N}_{b,\alpha} in terms of the complex variables UeU_{e}, UiU_{i}, and UbU_{b}. Indeed, it follows from (3.8) that

n=−|∇|ε−1/21+R2​Λe​(Ue+Ue¯)+|∇|ε−1/2R1+R2​Λi​(Ui+Ui¯),ρ=|∇|​R1+R2​Λe​(Ue+Ue¯)+|∇|1+R2​Λi​(Ui+Ui¯),h=iε−1/21+R2​(Ue−Ue¯)+−iε−1/2R1+R2​(Ui−Ui¯),g=−i​R1+R2​(Ue−Ue¯)+−i1+R2​(Ui−Ui¯)Aα=Λb−1​(Ub,α+Ub,α¯).\begin{split}&n=\frac{-|\nabla|\varepsilon^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}\Lambda_{e}}(U_{e}+\overline{U_{e}})+\frac{|\nabla|\varepsilon^{-1/2}R}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}\Lambda_{i}}(U_{i}+\overline{U_{i}}),\\ &\rho=\frac{|\nabla|R}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}\Lambda_{e}}(U_{e}+\overline{U_{e}})+\frac{|\nabla|}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}\Lambda_{i}}(U_{i}+\overline{U_{i}}),\\ &h=\frac{i\varepsilon^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}(U_{e}-\overline{U_{e}})+\frac{-i\varepsilon^{-1/2}R}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}(U_{i}-\overline{U_{i}}),\\ &g=\frac{-iR}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}(U_{e}-\overline{U_{e}})+\frac{-i}{\sqrt{1+R^{2}}}(U_{i}-\overline{U_{i}})\\ &A_{\alpha}=\Lambda_{b}^{-1}(U_{b,\alpha}+\overline{U_{b,\alpha}}).\end{split} (3.11)

We summarize now the main results we proved in this section. Recall first the definitions of the main multipliers

Λe(ξ):=ε−1/2(1+ε)+(T+ε)​|ξ|2+((1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2)2+4​ε2,Λi(ξ):=ε−1/2(1+ε)+(T+ε)​|ξ|2−((1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2)2+4​ε2,Λb(ξ):=ε−1/21+ε+Cb​|ξ|2,\begin{split}&\Lambda_{e}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{\frac{(1+\varepsilon)+(T+\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}+\sqrt{\left((1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}\right)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}{2}},\\ &\Lambda_{i}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{\frac{(1+\varepsilon)+(T+\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}-\sqrt{\left((1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}\right)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}{2}},\\ &\Lambda_{b}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+\varepsilon+C_{b}|\xi|^{2}},\\ \end{split} (3.12)

and

|∇|(ξ):=|ξ|,Rα(ξ):=iξα/|ξ|,Qα​β(ξ):=i∈α​γ​βξγ/|ξ|,H1(ξ):=1+|ξ|2,Hε(ξ):=ε−1/21+T​|ξ|2,R(ξ):=[Λe(ξ)2−Hε(ξ)2]1/2[Hε(ξ)2−Λi(ξ)]−1/2.\begin{split}&|\nabla|(\xi):=|\xi|,\qquad R_{\alpha}(\xi):=i\xi_{\alpha}/|\xi|,\qquad Q_{\alpha\beta}(\xi):=i\in_{\alpha\gamma\beta}\xi_{\gamma}/|\xi|,\qquad H_{1}(\xi):=\sqrt{1+|\xi|^{2}},\\ &H_{\varepsilon}(\xi):=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+T|\xi|^{2}},\qquad R(\xi):=[\Lambda_{e}(\xi)^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}(\xi)^{2}]^{1/2}[H_{\varepsilon}(\xi)^{2}-\Lambda_{i}(\xi)]^{-1/2}.\end{split} (3.13)

The lemma below describes symbol-type properties of some of these multipliers.

Lemma 3.1.

In ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} we have

Λe2≥Hε2≥H12≥Λi2≥|∇|2,Λi2≲|∇|2,\Lambda_{e}^{2}\geq H_{\varepsilon}^{2}\geq H_{1}^{2}\geq\Lambda_{i}^{2}\geq|\nabla|^{2},\qquad\Lambda_{i}^{2}\lesssim|\nabla|^{2}, (3.14)

and

Λe2−Hε2=ε−1/2R,Hε2−Λi2=ε−1/2R−1,Λe​(ξ)2−Hε​(ξ)2=H1​(ξ)2−Λi​(ξ)2=2(1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2+((1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2)2+4​ε.\begin{split}&\Lambda_{e}^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}^{2}=\varepsilon^{-1/2}R,\qquad H_{\varepsilon}^{2}-\Lambda_{i}^{2}=\varepsilon^{-1/2}R^{-1},\\ &\Lambda_{e}(\xi)^{2}-H_{\varepsilon}(\xi)^{2}=H_{1}(\xi)^{2}-\Lambda_{i}(\xi)^{2}=\frac{2}{(1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}+\sqrt{\big((1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}\big)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}.\end{split} (3.15)

|DαξΛe(ξ)|+|DαξHε(ξ)|+|DαξH1(ξ)|≲|α|(1+|ξ|)1−|α|,|DαξΛi(ξ)|+|Dαξ|∇|(ξ)|≲|α||ξ|1−|α|,|DαξR(ξ)|≲|α|(1+|ξ|)−2−|α|.\begin{split}&|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}\Lambda_{e}(\xi)|+|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}H_{\varepsilon}(\xi)|+|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}H_{1}(\xi)|\lesssim_{|\alpha|}(1+|\xi|)^{1-|\alpha|},\\ &|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}\Lambda_{i}(\xi)|+|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}|\nabla|(\xi)|\lesssim_{|\alpha|}|\xi|^{1-|\alpha|},\\ &|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}R(\xi)|\lesssim_{|\alpha|}(1+|\xi|)^{-2-|\alpha|}.\end{split} (3.16)
Proof of Lemma 3.1.

The inequalities in (3.14) and the identities in (3.15) follow directly from definitions. The symbol-type estimates in (3.16) also follow from definitions and the additional formula

R⁡(ξ)=2​ε1/2(1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2+((1−ε)+(T−ε)​|ξ|2)2+4​ε.R(\xi)=\frac{2\varepsilon^{1/2}}{(1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}+\sqrt{\big((1-\varepsilon)+(T-\varepsilon)|\xi|^{2}\big)^{2}+4\varepsilon}}.

∎

The following proposition is the main result in this section.

Proposition 3.2.

With N0=104N_{0}=10^{4} as in Theorem 1.1, assume that (n,v,ρ,u,E~,B~)∈C⁡(I:H~N0)(n,v,\rho,u,\tilde{E},\tilde{B})\in C(I:\widetilde{H}^{N_{0}}) is a solution of the system (1.8)-(1.10), where I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R} is an interval. Let Λe,Λi,Λb,|∇|,Rα,Q,H1,Hε,R\Lambda_{e},\Lambda_{i},\Lambda_{b},|\nabla|,R_{\alpha},Q,H_{1},H_{\varepsilon},R denote the operators defined by the corresponding multipliers in (3.12)-(3.13). Let

The claim (3.18) is a consequence of (3.16) and the observation that R⁡(0)=ε1/2R(0)=\varepsilon^{1/2}. The diagonalized dispersive system (3.19) and the identities (3.22) were derived earlier, see (3.9)-(3.10), (3.2), and (3.11). It remains only to prove the formulas (3.20), showing that the nonlinearities 𝒩e,𝒩i,𝒩b\mathcal{N}_{e},\mathcal{N}_{i},\mathcal{N}_{b} can be expressed as bilinear forms in terms of the complex variables Ue,Ui,UbU_{e},U_{i},U_{b}. The precise formulas of the multipliers me;μ,νm_{e;\mu,\nu}, mi;μ,νm_{i;\mu,\nu}, and mb;μ,νm_{b;\mu,\nu}, derived in section C below, are complicated. However, we do not use these formulas in the rest of the paper. We will only use the simple observation that these multipliers can be expressed as suitable products of multipliers satisfying inequalities of the Hörmander–Michlin type. More precisely, for any integer n≥1n\geq 1 let

𝒮n:={q:ℝ3→ℂ:∥q∥𝒮n:=supξ∈ℝ3∖{0}sup|α|≤n|ξ||α||Dξαq(ξ)|<∞},\mathcal{S}^{n}:=\{q:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}:\,\|q\|_{\mathcal{S}^{n}}:=\sup_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\}}\sup_{|\alpha|\leq n}|\xi|^{|\alpha|}|D^{\alpha}_{\xi}q(\xi)|<\infty\}, (3.23)

The multipliers me;μ,ν​(ξ,η)m_{e;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta) and mb,α;μ,ν​(ξ,η)m_{b,\alpha;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta), α∈{1,2,3}\alpha\in\{1,2,3\}, can be written as finite sums of functions of the form

Similarly, the multipliers mi;μ,ν​(ξ,η)m_{i;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta) can be written as finite sums of functions of the form

|ξ|⋅m⁡(ξ,η),m∈ℳ.|\xi|\cdot m(\xi,\eta),\qquad m\in\mathcal{M}. (3.26)
Remark 3.4.

We notice that the multipliers mi;μ,νm_{i;\mu,\nu} satisfy better estimates at ξ=0\xi=0 than the multipliers me;μ,νm_{e;\mu,\nu} and mb,α;μ,νm_{b,\alpha;\mu,\nu}; in particular these multipliers vanish at the origin. This is an indication of a certain null structure of the system, and is important in the analysis in sections 5 and 6.

The formulas (3.25) and (3.26) follow from the identities (3.10)-(3.11) and Lemma 3.1. 4. Main definitions and propositions

In this section we define our main function spaces, and state two key propositions that concern properties of solutions of the dispersive system (3.19). Then we show how to use these propositions, together with the local regularity theory in section 2 and linear dispersive bounds, to complete the proof of the main theorem.

We will prove the key bound (5.11) in several steps. The main ingredients in the proof are the estimates (5.15)–(5.18) above, together with (A.60). In this subsection we start by considering some of the easier cases, and reduce matters to proving Proposition 5.4 below. In all the cases analyzed in this subsection we can in fact control the stronger norm Bk,jσ,1B^{\sigma,1}_{k,j}, see Definition 4.1, instead of the required Bk,jσB^{\sigma}_{k,j} norm.

Lemma 5.2.

With D=D⁡(ε,T,Cb)D=D(\varepsilon,T,C_{b}) sufficiently large, the estimate

∑(k1,j1),(k2,j2)∈𝒥(1+2k)​2kσ​‖φ~j(k)⋅Pk​Tmσ;μ,ν​(fk1,j1μ,fk2,j2ν)‖Bk,j1≲2−β4​m\sum_{(k_{1},j_{1}),(k_{2},j_{2})\in\mathcal{J}}(1+2^{k})2^{k_{\sigma}}\big\|\widetilde{\varphi}^{(k)}_{j}\cdot P_{k}T_{m}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(f^{\mu}_{k_{1},j_{1}},f^{\nu}_{k_{2},j_{2}})\big\|_{B^{1}_{k,j}}\lesssim 2^{-\beta^{4}m} (5.23)

Therefore, using Plancherel theorem,

It follows that the left-hand side of (5.26) is dominated by

when k≤0k\leq 0, and by

5.3. Proof of Proposition 5.4

In this subsection we will show that proving Proposition 5.4 can be further reduced to proving Proposition 5.9 below. The arguments are more complicated than before, and we need to examine our bilinear operators more carefully; however, in all cases discussed in this subsection we can still control the stronger Bk,j1B^{1}_{k,j} norms.

We notice that we are looking to prove the bound (5.33) for fixed k,j,k1,j1,k2,j2,mk,j,k_{1},j_{1},k_{2},j_{2},m. We will consider several cases, depending on the relative sizes of these parameters.

Lemma 5.5.

j≥max⁡(m+D,−k⁡(1+β2)+D).j\geq\max(m+D,-k(1+\beta^{2})+D). (5.35)

The rest of the section is concerned with the proof of Proposition 6.1. The interactions corresponding to Case A are among the most difficult to control. A key element we need is a precise description of the sizes of the various elements close to the resonant set. This is made possible by the fact that the Hessian of the phases is nondegenerate. We refer to the introduction of [29] for more details.

In this section we consider type B interactions, see Proposition B.2, and prove the following proposition:

Proposition 7.1.

Appendix A General estimates and the functions Λi,Λe,Λb\Lambda_{i},\Lambda_{e},\Lambda_{b}

In this section we summarize the linear and the bilinear estimates we use in the paper. We also provide precise descriptions of the eigenvalues Λi,Λe,Λb\Lambda_{i},\Lambda_{e},\Lambda_{b} defined in (3.12).

We note first that Calderon–Zygmund operators are compatible with the spaces constructed in Definition 4.1. More precisely:

Lemma A.1.

Assume q∈𝒮10q\in\mathcal{S}^{10}, see (3.23), and Tq​f:=ℱ−1​(q⋅f^)T_{q}f:=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(q\cdot\widehat{f}). Then

‖Tq​f‖Z≲‖q‖𝒮10​‖f‖Z, for any ​f∈Z.\|T_{q}f\|_{Z}\lesssim\|q\|_{\mathcal{S}^{10}}\|f\|_{Z},\qquad\text{ for any }f\in Z.

We omit the proof of this lemma, since it is identical to the proof of Lemma 5.1 in [29]. The following general oscillatory integral estimate is used repeatedly in the proofs.

Lemma A.2.

Assume that 0<ϵ≤1/ϵ≤K0<\epsilon\leq 1/\epsilon\leq K, N≥1N\geq 1 is an integer, and f,g∈CN​(ℝn)f,g\in C^{N}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). Then

|∫ℝnei​K​fgdx|≲N(Kϵ)−N[∑|ρ|≤Nϵ|ρ|∥Dxρg∥L1],\Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}e^{iKf}g\,dx\Big|\lesssim_{N}(K\epsilon)^{-N}\big[\sum_{|\rho|\leq N}\epsilon^{|\rho|}\|D^{\rho}_{x}g\|_{L^{1}}\big], (A.1)

provided that ff is real-valued,

|∇xf|≥𝟏supp​g, and ∥Dxρf⋅𝟏supp​g∥L∞≲Nϵ1−|ρ|, 2≤|ρ|≤N.|\nabla_{x}f|\geq\mathbf{1}_{{\mathrm{supp}}\,g},\quad\text{ and }\quad\|D_{x}^{\rho}f\cdot\mathbf{1}_{{\mathrm{supp}}\,g}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{N}\epsilon^{1-|\rho|},\,2\leq|\rho|\leq N. (A.2)
Proof of Lemma A.2.

We localize first to balls of size ≈ϵ\approx\epsilon. Using the assumptions in (A.2) we may assume that inside each small ball, one of the directional derivatives of ff is bounded away from 00, say |∂1f|≳N1|\partial_{1}f|\gtrsim_{N}1. Then we integrate by parts NN times in x1x_{1}, and the desired bound (A.1) follows. ∎

We will also use repeatedly the following simple bilinear estimate:

Lemma A.3.

Assume p,q∈[2,∞]p,q\in[2,\infty] satisfy 1/p+1/q=1/21/p+1/q=1/2, and m∈L∞​(ℝ3×ℝ3)m\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}). Then, for any f,g∈L2​(ℝ3)f,g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),

‖∫ℝ3m⁡(ξ,η)⋅f^​(ξ−η)​g^​(η)​𝑑η‖Lξ2≲‖ℱ−1​m‖L1​(ℝ3×ℝ3)​‖f‖Lp​‖g‖Lq.\Big\|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}m(\xi,\eta)\cdot\widehat{f}(\xi-\eta)\widehat{g}(\eta)\,d\eta\Big\|_{L^{2}_{\xi}}\lesssim\|\mathcal{F}^{-1}m\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}\|f\|_{L^{p}}\|g\|_{L^{q}}. (A.3)
Proof of Lemma A.3.

Let

K⁡(x,y):=(ℱ−1​m)​(x,y)=∫ℝ3×ℝ3m⁡(ξ,η)​ei​x⋅ξ​ei​y⋅η​𝑑ξ​𝑑η.K(x,y):=(\mathcal{F}^{-1}m)(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}m(\xi,\eta)e^{ix\cdot\xi}e^{iy\cdot\eta}\,d\xi d\eta.

Then, for any h∈C0∞​(ℝ3)h\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) we estimate

|∫ℝ3×ℝ3m⁡(ξ,η)​f^​(ξ−η)⋅g^​(η)​h^​(ξ)​𝑑ξ​𝑑η|=C​|∫ℝ3×ℝ3×ℝ3f⁡(x)​g​(y)​h​(z)⋅K⁡(−x−z,x−y)​𝑑x​𝑑y​𝑑z|≲∫ℝ3×ℝ3×ℝ3|f⁡(x)​g​(x−v)​h​(−x−u)|⋅|K⁡(u,v)|​𝑑x​𝑑u​𝑑v≲‖K‖L1​(ℝ3×ℝ3)⋅‖f‖Lp​‖g‖Lq​‖h‖L2,\begin{split}\Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}m(\xi,\eta)\widehat{f}(\xi-\eta)\cdot\widehat{g}(\eta)\widehat{h}(\xi)\,d\xi d\eta\Big|&=C\Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}f(x)g(y)h(z)\cdot K(-x-z,x-y)\,dxdydz\Big|\\ &\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}|f(x)g(x-v)h(-x-u)|\cdot|K(u,v)|\,dxdudv\\ &\lesssim\|K\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}\cdot\|f\|_{L^{p}}\|g\|_{L^{q}}\|h\|_{L^{2}},\end{split}

and the desired bound (A.3) follows. ∎

Our last lemma in this section is a bilinear estimate. Recall the operators Qsσ;μ,νQ_{s}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu} defined in (5.4),

Φσ;μ,ν​(ξ,η)=∫0|ξ−η|λi′​(s)​𝑑s+∫0|ξ|λb′​(s)​𝑑s−∫0|η|λe′​(s)​𝑑s≥CCb,ε−1+|ξ−η|​λi′​(|ξ−η|)−(|η|−|ξ|)​λe′​(|η|)≳Cb,ε1.\begin{split}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)&=\int_{0}^{|\xi-\eta|}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(s)\,ds+\int_{0}^{|\xi|}\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(s)\,ds-\int_{0}^{|\eta|}\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(s)\,ds\\ &\geq C_{C_{b},\varepsilon}^{-1}+|\xi-\eta|\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(|\xi-\eta|)-(|\eta|-|\xi|)\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(|\eta|)\\ &\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1.\end{split}

This provides the contradiction. ∎

We consider now the remaining 20 phases, and define three sets of phases

𝒯A:={Φi;i−,e+,Φi;i−,b+,Φi;e+,b−,Φi;e−,b+,Φe;i+,e+,Φe;i+,b+,Φe;i−,b+,Φe;e−,b+,Φb;i+,e+,Φb;i+,b+,Φb;e+,e+,Φb;e+,b+,Φb;e−,b+},𝒯B:={Φe;i+,e+,Φe;i−,e+,Φb;i+,b+,Φb;i−,b+},𝒯C:={Φi;i+,i+,Φi;i+,i−,Φi;i−,i−,Φi;e+,e−,Φi;e+,b−,Φi;e−,b+,Φi;b+,b−}.\begin{split}\mathcal{T}_{A}:=&\{\Phi^{i;i-,e+},\Phi^{i;i-,b+},\Phi^{i;e+,b-},\Phi^{i;e-,b+},\Phi^{e;i+,e+},\Phi^{e;i+,b+},\Phi^{e;i-,b+},\Phi^{e;e-,b+},\\ &\,\,\Phi^{b;i+,e+},\Phi^{b;i+,b+},\Phi^{b;e+,e+},\Phi^{b;e+,b+},\Phi^{b;e-,b+}\},\\ \mathcal{T}_{B}:=&\{\Phi^{e;i+,e+},\Phi^{e;i-,e+},\Phi^{b;i+,b+},\Phi^{b;i-,b+}\},\\ \mathcal{T}_{C}:=&\{\Phi^{i;i+,i+},\Phi^{i;i+,i-},\Phi^{i;i-,i-},\Phi^{i;e+,e-},\Phi^{i;e+,b-},\Phi^{i;e-,b+},\Phi^{i;b+,b-}\}.\end{split} (B.7)

Notice that some phases, such as Φe;i+,e+\Phi^{e;i+,e+}, belong to more than one set. The set 𝒯A\mathcal{T}_{A} corresponds to phases having nondegenerate stationary points on spheres, while the sets 𝒯B,𝒯C\mathcal{T}_{B},\mathcal{T}_{C} consist of phases with degenerate behavior around 00 (in η\eta, ξ−η\xi-\eta, or ξ\xi). More precisely:

Proposition B.2.

Assume k,k1,k2∈ℤk,k_{1},k_{2}\in\mathbb{Z} and that there is a point (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} satisfying

|Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤δ1=2−10​D​2−4​max⁡(0,k1,k2),|Φσ;μ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤δ2=2−10​D​2−max⁡(0,k1,k2).|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq\delta_{1}=2^{-10D}2^{-4\max(0,k_{1},k_{2})},\quad|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq\delta_{2}=2^{-10D}2^{-\max(0,k_{1},k_{2})}.

Then one of the three following possibilities holds:

Case A: −D/2≤k,k1,k2≤D/2-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2 and Φσ;μ,ν∈∈𝒯A\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\mathcal{T}_{A}.

Case B: min(k1,k2)≤−D/3\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq-D/3, k≥−D/4k\geq-D/4 and Φσ;μ,ν∈∈𝒯B\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\mathcal{T}_{B}.

Case C: k≤−D/4k\leq-D/4 and Φσ;μ,ν∈∈𝒯C\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\mathcal{T}_{C}.

Proof of Proposition B.2.

We divide the proof in several steps:

Step 1. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;i+,i+,Φi;i+,i−,Φi;i−,i−}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;i+,i+},\Phi^{i;i+,i-},\Phi^{i;i-,i-}\}. (B.8)

These phases are only in the set 𝒯C\mathcal{T}_{C}, and we have to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

k≤−D/2.k\leq-D/2. (B.9)

Assume for contradiction that k≥−D/2k\geq-D/2. Using Lemma A.4 (iii) it is easy to see that if Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;i−,i−}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;i-,i-}\} then |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳ε,Cbmax(|ξ|,|η|,|ξ−η|)≳ε,Cb2−D/2|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{\varepsilon,C_{b}}\max(|\xi|,|\eta|,|\xi-\eta|)\gtrsim_{\varepsilon,C_{b}}2^{-D/2}, which is not possible. On the other hand, if min⁡(k1,k2)≤−5​D\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq-5D and max(k1,k2)≥−D/2−10\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D/2-10, then we use the bound

λi′​(r)−λi′​(s)≥qi​(0)−CCb,ε​r−qi​(s)≥2−2​D,\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(r)-\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(s)\geq q_{i}(0)-C_{C_{b},\varepsilon}r-q_{i}(s)\geq 2^{-2D},

whenever 0≤r≤2−4​D0\leq r\leq 2^{-4D} and s≥2−Ds\geq 2^{-D}, which is a consequence of Lemma A.4 (iii). Therefore, in this case |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≥2−2​D|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\geq 2^{-2D} for all (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}}, which provides the contradiction.

Step 2. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;e+,e−,Φi;b+,b−}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;e+,e-},\Phi^{i;b+,b-}\}. (B.10)

These phases are only in the set 𝒯C\mathcal{T}_{C}, and it suffices to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

k≤−D/2.k\leq-D/2. (B.11)

Assume for contradiction that k≥−D/2k\geq-D/2. Since λσ′​(0)=0\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(0)=0, σ∈{e,b}\sigma\in\{e,b\}, the restriction |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤δ1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq\delta_{1} shows that min⁡(k1,k2)≥−D\min(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D. On the other hand, if min⁡(k,k1,k2)≥−D\min(k,k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D then, for any (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} we have

|Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε|λσ′(|η−ξ|)−λσ′(|η|)|+max[λσ′(|η−ξ|),λσ′(|η|)]|η−ξ|η−ξ|−η|η||≥2Dδ1,|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}\big|\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta-\xi|)-\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta|)\big|+\max[\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta-\xi|),\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta|)]\Big|\frac{\eta-\xi}{|\eta-\xi|}-\frac{\eta}{|\eta|}\Big|\geq 2^{D}\delta_{1},

which provides a contradiction.

Step 3. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;e+,b−,Φi;e−,b+}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;e+,b-},\Phi^{i;e-,b+}\}. (B.12)

These phases are in the sets 𝒯C\mathcal{T}_{C} and 𝒯A\mathcal{T}_{A}, and we have to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

 either k≤−D/4 or −D/2≤k,k1,k2≤D/2.\text{ either }\qquad k\leq-D/4\qquad\text{ or }\qquad-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2.

This is equivalent to proving that

 if k≥−D/4 and ℒσ;μ,νk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2≠∅ then −D/2≤k,k1,k2≤D/2.\text{ if }\quad k\geq-D/4\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset\quad\text{ then }\quad-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2. (B.13)

Since

limr→∞λi′​(r)=1,limr→∞λe′​(r)=T/ε,limr→∞λb′​(r)=Cb/ε,\lim_{r\to\infty}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(r)=1,\qquad\lim_{r\to\infty}\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(r)=\sqrt{T/\varepsilon},\qquad\lim_{r\to\infty}\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(r)=\sqrt{C_{b}/\varepsilon}, (B.14)

it is easy to see that the condition ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset implies that max⁡(k1,k2,k3)≤D/4\max(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3})\leq D/4. Since k≥−D/4k\geq-D/4 it follows that max(k1,k2)≥−D/4−10\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D/4-10. Recall that λσ′​(0)=0\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(0)=0 and λσ′′(r)≈Cb,ε(1+r2)−3/2\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{\sigma}(r)\approx_{C_{b},\varepsilon}(1+r^{2})^{-3/2}, σ∈{e,b}\sigma\in\{e,b\} (see Lemma A.4 (i)). Since |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤δ1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq\delta_{1} for some (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} it follows that min(k1,k2)≥−D/2\min(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D/2 as desired.

Step 4. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φe;i−,e+,Φb;i−,b+}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{e;i-,e+},\Phi^{b;i-,b+}\}. (B.15)

These phases are only in the set 𝒯B\mathcal{T}_{B}, and we have to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

k≥−D/4 and min(k1,k2)≤−D/3.k\geq-D/4\,\,\text{ and }\,\,\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq-D/3. (B.16)

It is easy to see that max(k1,k2,k)≥−D/10\max(k_{1},k_{2},k)\geq-D/10; otherwise |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≥2−2​D|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\geq 2^{-2D} for all (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}}, in view of the fact that λe′​(0)=λb′​(0)=0\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(0)=\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(0)=0 and λi′(0)≈Cb,ε1\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(0)\approx_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1. Therefore it remains to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

min(k1,k2)≤−D/3.\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq-D/3. (B.17)

Assume, for contradiction, that (B.17) fails. We may assume, without loss of generality, that

Φσ;μ,ν​(ξ,η)=Φσ;i−,σ+​(ξ,η)=λσ​(|ξ|)+λi​(|ξ−η|)−λσ​(|η|),\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)=\Phi^{\sigma;i-,\sigma+}(\xi,\eta)=\lambda_{\sigma}(|\xi|)+\lambda_{i}(|\xi-\eta|)-\lambda_{\sigma}(|\eta|),

for σ∈{e,b}\sigma\in\{e,b\}. We argue as in the proof of Lemma B.1, Φσ;μ,ν=Φb;i−,e+∈𝒯N​R\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}=\Phi^{b;i-,e+}\in\mathcal{T}_{NR}. The conditions |Φσ;μ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤2−10​D|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq 2^{-10D} and k1≥−D/3k_{1}\geq-D/3 show that |η|≥|ξ||\eta|\geq|\xi|. Since

λi′​(r)≤1+T1+ε and λb′​(r)≥λe′​(r)≥(1−ε)​T​rε​1+T​r2,\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(r)\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+T}}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(r)\geq\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(r)\geq\frac{(1-\sqrt{\varepsilon})Tr}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}\sqrt{1+Tr^{2}}},

for any r∈[0,∞)r\in[0,\infty), see Lemma A.4 (ii) and (iii), the restriction |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≤2−D|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\leq 2^{-D} shows that |η|≤ε/T|\eta|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon/T}. Since r∗≥T−1/2r_{\ast}\geq T^{-1/2}, see Lemma A.4 (i), it follows that |ξ−η|≤r∗/2|\xi-\eta|\leq r_{\ast}/2. Therefore λi′\lambda^{\prime}_{i} is decreasing on the interval [0,|ξ−η|][0,|\xi-\eta|] and we estimate, recalling that 2−10​D≥|Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≥|λi′​(|ξ−η|)−λσ′​(|η|)|2^{-10D}\geq\big|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)\big|\geq\big|\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(|\xi-\eta|)-\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta|)\big| and |ξ−η|≥2−D/2|\xi-\eta|\geq 2^{-D/2},

Φσ;μ,ν​(ξ,η)=∫0|ξ−η|λi′​(s)​𝑑s−∫|ξ||η|λσ′​(s)​𝑑s≥2−2​D+|ξ−η|​λi′​(|ξ−η|)−(|η|−|ξ|)​λσ′​(|η|)≥2−4​D.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)=\int_{0}^{|\xi-\eta|}\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(s)\,ds-\int_{|\xi|}^{|\eta|}\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(s)\,ds\geq 2^{-2D}+|\xi-\eta|\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(|\xi-\eta|)-(|\eta|-|\xi|)\lambda^{\prime}_{\sigma}(|\eta|)\geq 2^{-4D}.

This provides the contradiction.

Step 5. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φe;i+,e+,Φb;i+,b+}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{e;i+,e+},\Phi^{b;i+,b+}\}. (B.18)

These phases are in the sets 𝒯B\mathcal{T}_{B} and 𝒯A\mathcal{T}_{A}, and we have to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

 either k≥−D/4,min(k1,k2)≤−D/3 or −D/2≤k,k1,k2≤D/2.\text{ either }\qquad k\geq-D/4,\,\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq-D/3\qquad\text{ or }\qquad-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2. (B.19)

 if min(k1,k2)≥−D/3 then −D/2≤k,k1,k2≤D/2.\text{ if }\qquad\min(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D/3\qquad\text{ then }\qquad-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2. (B.20)

In view of (B.14), it is clear that min⁡(k1,k2)≤D/10\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq D/10; otherwise |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)|≥2−2​D|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\geq 2^{-2D} for all (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}}. On the other hand, if k≥D/4k\geq D/4 then max⁡(k1,k2)≥D/4−10\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq D/4-10, and one can use (B.14) again to see easily that this in contradiction with the assumption ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset. Step 6. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φe;e−,b+,Φb;e+,e+,Φb;e+,b+,Φb;e−,b+}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{e;e-,b+},\Phi^{b;e+,e+},\Phi^{b;e+,b+},\Phi^{b;e-,b+}\}. (B.21)

−D/2≤k,k1,k2-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2} (B.22)

and

We prove now (B.23). We notice first that min⁡(k,k1,k2)≤D/10\min(k,k_{1},k_{2})\leq D/10; otherwise either |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 or |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 for any (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}}, using (B.14). Assuming, for contradiction, that (B.23) fails, we need to consider two cases:

 either k≤D/10,max(k1,k2)≥D/2,|k1−k2|≤10, or min(k1,k2)≤D/10,max(k,k1,k2)≥D/2,|k−max(k1,k2)|≤10.\begin{split}\text{ either }\qquad&k\leq D/10,\quad\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq D/2,\quad|k_{1}-k_{2}|\leq 10,\\ \text{ or }\qquad&\min(k_{1},k_{2})\leq D/10,\quad\max(k,k_{1},k_{2})\geq D/2,\quad|k-\max(k_{1},k_{2})|\leq 10.\end{split} (B.25)

In the first case, we use (B.14) to see that |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 for any (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} if Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φe;e−,b+,Φb;e+,b+,Φb;e−,b+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{e;e-,b+},\Phi^{b;e+,b+},\Phi^{b;e-,b+}\}. We also notice that |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 for any (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} if Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φb;e+,e+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{b;e+,e+}\}, which completes the contradiction in this case.

Assume now that the inequalities in the second line of (B.25) hold. By symmetry we may assume that k1=min⁡(k1,k2)k_{1}=\min(k_{1},k_{2}). In view of (B.14) it is clear that |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φe;e−,b+,Φb;e+,b+,Φb;e−,b+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{e;e-,b+},\Phi^{b;e+,b+},\Phi^{b;e-,b+}\}. Also, using (B.5) it is clear that |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φe;,b+,e−,Φb;e+,e+,Φb;b+,e+,Φb;b+,e−}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{e;,b+,e-},\Phi^{b;e+,e+},\Phi^{b;b+,e+},\Phi^{b;b+,e-}\}. This completes the contradiction in this case as well, and the desired bound (B.23) follows.

Step 7. Assume that

Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;i−,e+,Φi;i−,b+,Φe;i+,b+,Φe;i−,b+,Φb;i+,e+}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;i-,e+},\Phi^{i;i-,b+},\Phi^{e;i+,b+},\Phi^{e;i-,b+},\Phi^{b;i+,e+}\}. (B.26)

These phases are only in the set 𝒯A\mathcal{T}_{A}, and we have to prove that if ℒk,k1,k2;δ1,δ2σ;μ,ν≠∅\mathcal{L}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{k,k_{1},k_{2};\delta_{1},\delta_{2}}\neq\emptyset then

−D/2≤k,k1,k2-D/2\leq k,k_{1},k_{2} (B.27)

and

k,k1,k2≤D/2.k,k_{1},k_{2}\leq D/2. (B.28)

To prove (B.28), assume, for contradiction, that max⁡(k1,k2)≥D/4\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq D/4. By symmetry, we may assume also k1≤k2k_{1}\leq k_{2}. Using (B.14) it is easy to see that |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φi;i−,e+,Φi;i−,b+,Φe;i+,b+,Φe;i−,b+,Φb;i+,e+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{i;i-,e+},\Phi^{i;i-,b+},\Phi^{e;i+,b+},\Phi^{e;i-,b+},\Phi^{b;i+,e+}\}. On the other hand, if

Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φi;,e+,i−,Φi;b+,i−,Φe;b+,i+,Φe;b+,i−,Φb;e+,i+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{i;,e+,i-},\Phi^{i;b+,i-},\Phi^{e;b+,i+},\Phi^{e;b+,i-},\Phi^{b;e+,i+}\}

then, using again (B.14) and the smallness of |Ξμ,ν​(ξ,η)||\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|, we necessarily have k1≤D/10k_{1}\leq D/10, |k−k2|≤10|k-k_{2}|\leq 10. In this case, however, |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1, as a consequence of (B.14). This completes the proof of the contradiction.

We prove now (B.27). We notice that max(k1,k2)≥−D/10\max(k_{1},k_{2})\geq-D/10; otherwise |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε1|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 for any (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}}, since λe′(0)=λb′(0)=0,λi′(0)≈Cb,ε1\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(0)=\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(0)=0,\,\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(0)\approx_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1. Assume, for contradiction, that (B.27) fails. We may assume by symmetry that k1≤k2k_{1}\leq k_{2} and need to consider two cases:

 either k1≤−D/2,k2≥−D/10,|k−k2|≤10, or k≤−D/2,k2≥−D/10,|k1−k2|≤10.\begin{split}\text{ either }\qquad&k_{1}\leq-D/2,\quad k_{2}\geq-D/10,\quad|k-k_{2}|\leq 10,\\ \text{ or }\qquad&k\leq-D/2,\quad k_{2}\geq-D/10,\quad|k_{1}-k_{2}|\leq 10.\end{split} (B.29)

Assume first that the inequalities in the first line of (B.29) hold. Since λi′(r)≈Cb,ε1\lambda^{\prime}_{i}(r)\approx_{C_{b},\varepsilon}1 and λb′​(0)=λe′​(0)=0\lambda^{\prime}_{b}(0)=\lambda^{\prime}_{e}(0)=0, it is easy to see that |Ξμ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε2−2​D|\Xi^{\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}2^{-2D} if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and

Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φi;e+,i−,Φi;b+,i−,Φe;b+,i+,Φe;b+,i−,Φb;e+,i+,}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{i;e+,i-},\Phi^{i;b+,i-},\Phi^{e;b+,i+},\Phi^{e;b+,i-},\Phi^{b;e+,i+},\}.

On the other hand, using (B.5), |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε2−2​D|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}2^{-2D} if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and

Φσ;μ,ν∈{Φi;i−,e+,Φi;i−,b+,Φe;i+,b+,Φe;i−,b+,Φb;i+,e+,}.\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\{\Phi^{i;i-,e+},\Phi^{i;i-,b+},\Phi^{e;i+,b+},\Phi^{e;i-,b+},\Phi^{b;i+,e+},\}.

The desired contradiction follows in this case.

Finally, assume that the inequalities in the second line of (B.29) hold. Using (B.5) it is easy to see that |Φσ;μ,ν(ξ,η)|≳Cb,ε2−2​D|\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)|\gtrsim_{C_{b},\varepsilon}2^{-2D} if (ξ,η)∈ℒk,k1,k2(\xi,\eta)\in\mathcal{L}_{k,k_{1},k_{2}} and Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φi;i−,e+,Φi;i−,b+,Φe;i+,b+,Φb;i+,e+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{i;i-,e+},\Phi^{i;i-,b+},\Phi^{e;i+,b+},\Phi^{b;i+,e+}\}. On the other hand, if Φσ;μ,ν∈∈{Φe;i−,b+}\Phi^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}\in\in\{\Phi^{e;i-,b+}\}, then the contradiction follows by the same argument as in Step 4. This completes the proof of the proposition. ∎

(Rα​g)⋅Aα=−iRRαUe+~⋅Λb−1[Ub+]α−iRRαUe+~⋅Λb−1[Ub−]α+iRRαUe−~⋅Λb−1[Ub+]α+iRRαUe−~⋅Λb−1[Ub−]α−iRαUi+~⋅Λb−1[Ub+]α−iRαUi+~⋅Λb−1[Ub−]α+iRαUi−~⋅Λb−1[Ub+]α+iRαUi−~⋅Λb−1[Ub−]α.\begin{split}(R_{\alpha}g)\cdot A_{\alpha}=&-iRR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{e+}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}-iRR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{e+}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}\\ &+iRR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{e-}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}+iRR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{e-}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}\\ &-iR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{i+}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}-iR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{i+}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}\\ &+iR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{i-}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}+iR_{\alpha}\widetilde{U_{i-}}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}.\end{split}

Finally,

Aα⋅Aα=Λb−1​[Ub+]α⋅Λb−1​[Ub+]α+2​Λb−1​[Ub+]α⋅Λb−1​[Ub−]α+Λb−1​[Ub−]α⋅Λb−1​[Ub−]α.\begin{split}A_{\alpha}\cdot A_{\alpha}&=\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}+2\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b+}\right]_{\alpha}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}+\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}\cdot\Lambda_{b}^{-1}\left[U_{b-}\right]_{\alpha}.\end{split}

Let

ℐ:={(e+,e+),(e+,e−),(e−,e−),(i+,i+),(i+,i−),(i−,i−),(b+α,b+β),(b+α,b−β),(b−α,b−β)(e+,i+),(e+,i−),(e−,i+),(e−,i−),(e+,b+α),(e+,b−α),(e−,b+α),(e−,b−α),(i+,b+α),(i+,b−α),(i−,b+α),(i−,b−α), 1≤α,β≤3}.\begin{split}\mathcal{I}:=&\big\{(e+,e+),(e+,e-),(e-,e-),(i+,i+),(i+,i-),(i-,i-),(b+\alpha,b+\beta),(b+\alpha,b-\beta),(b-\alpha,b-\beta)\\ &(e+,i+),(e+,i-),(e-,i+),(e-,i-),(e+,b+\alpha),(e+,b-\alpha),(e-,b+\alpha),(e-,b-\alpha),\\ &(i+,b+\alpha),(i+,b-\alpha),(i-,b+\alpha),(i-,b-\alpha),\,1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq 3\big\}.\end{split} (C.2)

The nonlinearities 𝒩e,𝒩i,𝒩b\mathcal{N}_{e},\mathcal{N}_{i},\mathcal{N}_{b} can be written in the form

ℱ⁡(𝒩e)​(ξ,t)=c​∑(μ,ν)∈ℐ∫ℝ3me;μ,ν​(ξ,η)​Uμ^​(ξ−η,t)​Uν^​(η,t)​dη,ℱ⁡(𝒩i)​(ξ,t)=c​∑(μ,ν)∈ℐ∫ℝ3mi;μ,ν​(ξ,η)​Uμ^​(ξ−η,t)​Uν^​(η,t)​𝑑ηℱ⁡(𝒩b,α)​(ξ,t)=c​∑(μ,ν)∈ℐ∫ℝ3mb,α;μ,ν​(ξ,η)​Uμ^​(ξ−η,t)​Uν^​(η,t)​dη.\begin{split}&\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{N}_{e})(\xi,t)=c\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{I}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}m_{e;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)\widehat{U_{\mu}}(\xi-\eta,t)\widehat{U_{\nu}}(\eta,t)\,d\eta,\\ &\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{N}_{i})(\xi,t)=c\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{I}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}m_{i;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)\widehat{U_{\mu}}(\xi-\eta,t)\widehat{U_{\nu}}(\eta,t)\,d\eta\\ &\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{N}_{b,\alpha})(\xi,t)=c\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{I}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}m_{b,\alpha;\mu,\nu}(\xi,\eta)\widehat{U_{\mu}}(\xi-\eta,t)\widehat{U_{\nu}}(\eta,t)\,d\eta.\end{split} (C.3)

Letting

Te;e,e​(ξ,η):=i[ε−1/2−R(ξ)R(ξ−η)R(η)](1+R​(ξ)2)​(1+R​(ξ−η)2)​(1+R​(η)2),Te;i,i​(ξ,η):=i[ε−1/2R(ξ−η)R(η)−R(ξ)](1+R​(ξ)2)​(1+R​(ξ−η)2)​(1+R​(η)2),Te;e,i​(ξ,η):=i[ε−1/2R(η)+R(ξ)R(ξ−η)](1+R​(ξ)2)​(1+R​(ξ−η)2)​(1+R​(η)2),Te;e,b​(ξ,η):=i⁡[−ε−1+R⁡(ξ)​R​(ξ−η)](1+R​(ξ)2)​(1+R​(ξ−η)2)​Λb​(η),Te;i,b​(ξ,η):=i⁡[ε−1​R​(ξ−η)+R⁡(ξ)](1+R​(ξ)2)​(1+R​(ξ−η)2)​Λb​(η),\begin{split}&T_{e;e,e}(\xi,\eta):=\frac{i[\varepsilon^{-1/2}-R(\xi)R(\xi-\eta)R(\eta)]}{\sqrt{(1+R(\xi)^{2})(1+R(\xi-\eta)^{2})(1+R(\eta)^{2})}},\\ &T_{e;i,i}(\xi,\eta):=\frac{i[\varepsilon^{-1/2}R(\xi-\eta)R(\eta)-R(\xi)]}{\sqrt{(1+R(\xi)^{2})(1+R(\xi-\eta)^{2})(1+R(\eta)^{2})}},\\ &T_{e;e,i}(\xi,\eta):=\frac{i[\varepsilon^{-1/2}R(\eta)+R(\xi)R(\xi-\eta)]}{\sqrt{(1+R(\xi)^{2})(1+R(\xi-\eta)^{2})(1+R(\eta)^{2})}},\\ &T_{e;e,b}(\xi,\eta):=\frac{i[-\varepsilon^{-1}+R(\xi)R(\xi-\eta)]}{\sqrt{(1+R(\xi)^{2})(1+R(\xi-\eta)^{2})}\Lambda_{b}(\eta)},\\ &T_{e;i,b}(\xi,\eta):=\frac{i[\varepsilon^{-1}R(\xi-\eta)+R(\xi)]}{\sqrt{(1+R(\xi)^{2})(1+R(\xi-\eta)^{2})}\Lambda_{b}(\eta)},\\ \end{split} (C.4)

the multipliers me;μ,νm_{e;\mu,\nu} are given by

me;e+,e+​(ξ,η)=Te;e,e​(ξ,η)​[+Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)4​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e+,e−​(ξ,η)=Te;e,e​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)+Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λe​(η)−|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e−,e−​(ξ,η)=Te;e,e​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)4​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;i+,i+​(ξ,η)=Te;i,i​(ξ,η)​[+Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λi​(ξ−η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)4​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;i+,i−​(ξ,η)=Te;i,i​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λi​(ξ−η)+Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λi​(η)−|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;i−,i−​(ξ,η)=Te;i,i​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λi​(ξ−η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)4​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e+,i+​(ξ,η)=Te;e,i​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)−Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λi​(η)−|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e+,i−​(ξ,η)=Te;e,i​(ξ,η)​[+Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)−Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λi​(η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e−,i+​(ξ,η)=Te;e,i​(ξ,η)​[−Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)+Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λi​(η)+|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|],me;e−,i−​(ξ,η)=Te;e,i​(ξ,η)​[+Λe​(ξ)​|ξ−η|​(ξ⋅η)2​|ξ|​|η|​Λe​(ξ−η)+Λe​(ξ)​|η|​(ξ⋅(ξ−η))2​|ξ|​|ξ−η|​Λi​(η)−|ξ|​((ξ−η)⋅η)2​|ξ−η|​|η|].\begin{split}&m_{e;e+,e+}(\xi,\eta)=T_{e;e,e}(\xi,\eta)\Big[+\frac{\Lambda_{e}(\xi)|\xi-\eta|(\xi\cdot\eta)}{2|\xi||\eta|\Lambda_{e}(\xi-\eta)}+\frac{|\xi|((\xi-\eta)\cdot\eta)}{4|\xi-\eta||\eta|}\Big],\\ &m_{e;e+,e-}(\xi,\eta)=T_{e;e,e}(\xi,\eta)\Big[-\frac{\Lambda_{e}(\xi)|\xi-\eta|(\xi\cdot\eta)}{2|\xi||\eta|\Lambda_{e}(\xi-\eta)}+\frac{\Lambda_{e}(\xi)|\eta|(\xi\cdot(\xi-\eta))}{2|\xi||\xi-\eta|\Lambda_{e}(\eta)}-\frac{|\xi|((\xi-\eta)\cdot\eta)}{2|\xi-\eta||\eta|}\Big],\\ &m_{e;i+,i+}(\xi,\eta)=T_{e;i,i}(\xi,\eta)\Big[+\frac{\Lambda_{e}(\xi)|\xi-\eta|(\xi\cdot\eta)}{2|\xi||\eta|\Lambda_{i}(\xi-\eta)}+\frac{|\xi|((\xi-\eta)\cdot\eta)}{4|\xi-\eta||\eta|}\Big],\\ Appendix D Other models

The purpose of this section is to show how the results in the main body of this work extend to several other models. In particular we focus on two variants of (1.1) which are invariant under appropriate change of frame: the Euler-Poisson is invariant under Galilean transformation, while the relativistic model is invariant under Lorentz transformations.

D.1. The Euler-Poisson model

Formally taking c→∞c\rightarrow\infty and B≡0B\equiv 0 in (1.1), we derive the Euler-Poisson system in the two-fluid theory, which is relevant when the magnetic forces can be neglected:

∂tne+div​(ne​ve)=0,ne​me​[∂tve+ve⋅∇ve]+∇pe=nee∇ϕ,∂tni+div​(ni​vi)=0,ni​Mi​[∂tvi+vi⋅∇vi]+∇pi=−Znie∇ϕ,−Δ​ϕ=4​π​e​(Z​ni−ne).\begin{split}\partial_{t}n_{e}+\hbox{div}(n_{e}v_{e})&=0,\\ n_{e}m_{e}\left[\partial_{t}v_{e}+v_{e}\cdot\nabla v_{e}\right]+\nabla p_{e}&=n_{e}e\nabla\phi,\\ \partial_{t}n_{i}+\hbox{div}(n_{i}v_{i})&=0,\\ n_{i}M_{i}\left[\partial_{t}v_{i}+v_{i}\cdot\nabla v_{i}\right]+\nabla p_{i}&=-Zn_{i}e\nabla\phi,\\ -\Delta\phi&=4\pi e(Zn_{i}-n_{e}).\end{split} (D.1)

Here the electromagnetic fields are given by

E=−∇ϕ,B=0.E=-\nabla\phi,\quad B=0.

Galilean invariance. This system is left invariant by Galilean change of unknowns. More precisely, let V∈ℝ3V\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be a fixed vector and let

x→x′:=x+V​t,t→t′:=tne→ne′:=ne,ve→ve′:=ve−V,ni→ni′:=ni,vi→vi′:=vi−V,ϕ→ϕ′:=ϕ,\begin{split}&x\to x^{\prime}:=x+Vt,\quad t\to t^{\prime}:=t\\ &n_{e}\to n_{e}^{\prime}:=n_{e},\quad v_{e}\to v_{e}^{\prime}:=v_{e}-V,\quad n_{i}\to n_{i}^{\prime}:=n_{i},\quad v_{i}\to v_{i}^{\prime}:=v_{i}-V,\quad\phi\to\phi^{\prime}:=\phi,\end{split}

then, we observe that (ne,ve,ni,vi,ϕ)​(x,t)(n_{e},v_{e},n_{i},v_{i},\phi)(x,t) solves (D.1) if and only if (ne′,ve′,ni′,vi′,ϕ′)​(x′,t′)(n_{e}^{\prime},v_{e}^{\prime},n_{i}^{\prime},v_{i}^{\prime},\phi^{\prime})(x^{\prime},t^{\prime}) does.

Theorem D.1.

Assume ε≤10−3\varepsilon\leq 10^{-3} and T∈[1/10,100]T\in[1/10,100]. Let N0=104N_{0}=10^{4} and assume that

D.1.1. Derivation and main steps of the proof.

The proof of this theorem is very similar to the proof of Theorem 1.1. Proposition 2.1 remains essentially unchanged using the energy

Note that qe′>0q_{e}^{\prime}>0 and qi′>0q_{i}^{\prime}>0 for small perturbations, as follows from (D.2) and (D.3) and that qe′​(0)=Tq_{e}^{\prime}(0)=T, qi′​(0)=1q_{i}^{\prime}(0)=1. This gives local existence of smooth solutions. Using that
