D.2. Relativistic model

We refer to [6, 20, 25] for other references about relativistic fluids.

D.2.1. Relativistic Euler-Maxwell model for the electron

As a starter, we introduce a simpler one-fluid relativistic Euler-Maxwell model, namely the model for the electrons. This is the relativistic counterpart of the (classical) Euler-Maxwell model for electrons already discussed in [14, 29].

We consider Minkowski space (ℝ1+3,gα​β)(\mathbb{R}^{1+3},g_{\alpha\beta}) with g00=−c2g_{00}=-c^{2}, gi​j=δi​jg_{ij}=\delta_{ij} and g0​j=gj​0=0g_{0j}=g_{j0}=0. Its inverse is denoted gμ​νg^{\mu\nu} where g00=−c−2g^{00}=-c^{-2}, gi​j=δi​jg^{ij}=\delta_{ij} and g0​j=0=gj​0g^{0j}=0=g^{j0}. We use the Einstein convention that repeated up-down indices be summed and we raise and lower indices using the metric. Latin indices i,j​…i,j\dots vary from 11 to 33, while greek indices μ,ν​…\mu,\nu\dots vary from 00 to 33.

We denote 𝒯d​(ℝ1+3)\mathcal{T}^{d}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}) the set of contravariant dd-tensors on the Minkowski space. We model the electron fluid by a scalar function ne∈𝒯0​(ℝ1+3)n_{e}\in\mathcal{T}^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}) and a velocity function u=(uα)0≤α≤3∈𝒯1​(ℝ1+3)u=(u^{\alpha})_{0\leq\alpha\leq 3}\in\mathcal{T}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}) normalized by1515 15 Some authors prefer to normalize the velocity of a particle of rest-mass mm by asking that uα​uα=−m​c2u^{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=-mc^{2}. Here, we prefer to incorporate the mass separately.

uα​uα=−c2.u^{\alpha}u_{\alpha}=-c^{2}. (D.15)

Below, we will always note γe=u0\gamma_{e}=u^{0} so that uν=(γe,v1,v2,v3)u^{\nu}=(\gamma_{e},v^{1},v^{2},v^{3}) with γe=1+c−2​|v|2\gamma_{e}=\sqrt{1+c^{-2}|v|^{2}}. We will repeatedly switch between uu and vv as one uniquely defines the other thanks to (D.15).

In addition, we also consider an electromagnetic field F={Fμ​ν}0≤μ,ν≤3∈𝒯2​(ℝ1+3)F=\{F^{\mu\nu}\}_{0\leq\mu,\nu\leq 3}\in\mathcal{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}). We assume that this field is skew-symmetric: Fμ​ν=−Fν​μF^{\mu\nu}=-F^{\nu\mu}. Finally, we also assume the presence of a uniform flat positively charged background of density of charge n0​en_{0}e and four-velocity ∂t=(1,0,0,0)∈𝒯1(ℝ1+3)\partial_{t}=(1,0,0,0)\in\mathcal{T}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}).

We can introduce the energy-momentum tensor associated to the fluid under consideration:

Tμ​ν=n​h​uμ​uνc2+p​gμ​ν∈𝒯2​(ℝ1+3),T^{\mu\nu}=nh\frac{u^{\mu}u^{\nu}}{c^{2}}+pg^{\mu\nu}\in\mathcal{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}),

h′​(x)=p′​(x)x,h⁡(0)=me​c2,h^{\prime}(x)=\frac{p^{\prime}(x)}{x},\quad h(0)=m_{e}c^{2}, (D.16)

where mem_{e} is the rest-mass of an electron. We can also consider the energy-momentum tensor of the electromagnetic field:

ℰμ​ν=−(4​π)−1​[Fμ​α​Fβ​ν​gα​β+14​Fα​β​Fα​β​gμ​ν]∈𝒯2​(ℝ1+3).\mathcal{E}^{\mu\nu}=-(4\pi)^{-1}\left[F^{\mu\alpha}F^{\beta\nu}g_{\alpha\beta}+\frac{1}{4}F^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta}g^{\mu\nu}\right]\in\mathcal{T}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{1+3}).

The dynamics are then given by three equations: the Maxwell equations, the continuity of matter and the balance of energy-momentum. The Maxwell equations give:

∂μFμ​ν=4​πc​Jν∂αFβ​γ+∂βFγ​α+∂γFα​β=0.\begin{split}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\frac{4\pi}{c}J^{\nu}\qquad\partial_{\alpha}F_{\beta\gamma}+\partial_{\beta}F_{\gamma\alpha}+\partial_{\gamma}F_{\alpha\beta}=0.\end{split} (D.17)

where the total relativistic current is defined by

The balance of Energy-momentum is then

∂νTμ​ν=e​nc​uα​Fμ​α.\begin{split}\partial_{\nu}T^{\mu\nu}=\frac{en}{c}u_{\alpha}F^{\mu\alpha}.\end{split}

This yields the following theorem:

Theorem D.2.

D.2.2. Relativistic Euler-Maxwell model for two fluids

Now we consider the relativistic analogue of (1.1). We consider again the standard Minkowski space (ℝ1+3,g)(\mathbb{R}^{1+3},g) defined as in the previous subsection.

The main unknowns are two densities nin_{i} and nen_{e}, two velocity fields viv_{i} and vev_{e} (both of which satisfy (D.15)) and an electromagnetic field FF. We are also given pressure laws pip_{i} and pep_{e} and enthalpies hih_{i} and heh_{e} satisfying (D.16), with MiM_{i}, the rest-mass of an ion instead of mem_{e} for pip_{i}, hih_{i}.

and we have two forms of balance of momentum:

ni​uiνc2​∂ν[hi​uiμ]+gμ​ν​∂νpi=−Z​e​nic​(ui)α​Fμ​αne​ueνc2​∂ν[he​ueμ]+gμ​ν​∂νpe=e​nec​(ue)α​Fμ​α.\begin{split}\frac{n_{i}u_{i}^{\nu}}{c^{2}}\partial_{\nu}\left[h_{i}u_{i}^{\mu}\right]+g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\nu}p_{i}=-Z\frac{en_{i}}{c}(u_{i})_{\alpha}F^{\mu\alpha}\\ \frac{n_{e}u_{e}^{\nu}}{c^{2}}\partial_{\nu}\left[h_{e}u_{e}^{\mu}\right]+g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\nu}p_{e}=\frac{en_{e}}{c}(u_{e})_{\alpha}F^{\mu\alpha}.\end{split} (D.29)

In particular, we recover the fact that the stress-energy tensor is divergence free1818 18 In general relativity, the stress energy tensor should be equated to a multiple of the Einstein tensor of space time. The fact that the stress energy tensor is divergence free is then a consequence of the Bianchi identity.

∂ν[Tiμ​ν+Teμ​ν+ℰμ​ν]=0,Tiμ​ν=nihiuiμ​uiνc2+pigμ​ν,Teμ​ν=neheueμ​ueνc2+pegμ​ν.\begin{split}&\partial_{\nu}\left[T_{i}^{\mu\nu}+T_{e}^{\mu\nu}+\mathcal{E}^{\mu\nu}\right]=0,\\ &T_{i}^{\mu\nu}=n_{i}h_{i}\frac{u^{\mu}_{i}u^{\nu}_{i}}{c^{2}}+p_{i}g^{\mu\nu},\qquad T_{e}^{\mu\nu}=n_{e}h_{e}\frac{u^{\mu}_{e}u^{\nu}_{e}}{c^{2}}+p_{e}g^{\mu\nu}.\end{split}

ωα​βi=∂α[hi​(ui)β]−∂β[hi​(ui)α]−Z​e​c​Fα​β,ωα​βe=∂α[he​(ue)β]−∂β[he​(ue)α]+e​c​Fα​β,\begin{split}\omega^{i}_{\alpha\beta}&=\partial_{\alpha}\left[h_{i}(u_{i})_{\beta}\right]-\partial_{\beta}\left[h_{i}(u_{i})_{\alpha}\right]-ZecF_{\alpha\beta},\\ \omega^{e}_{\alpha\beta}&=\partial_{\alpha}\left[h_{e}(u_{e})_{\beta}\right]-\partial_{\beta}\left[h_{e}(u_{e})_{\alpha}\right]+ecF_{\alpha\beta},\\ \end{split}

2k+⁣+​(2α​k+210​k)​2(1+β)​j​‖Pk​T~mσ;μ,ν​[fk1,j1μ,fk2,j2ν;Pk3​h]‖L2≲2−β​j.2^{k_{++}}(2^{\alpha k}+2^{10k})2^{(1+\beta)j}\|P_{k}\tilde{T}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{m}[f^{\mu}_{k_{1},j_{1}},f^{\nu}_{k_{2},j_{2}};P_{k_{3}}h]\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 2^{-\beta j}.

Together with (D.46), this finishes the proof in this case.

Finally, we may assume that

m/2+N0′​k+⁣++D2≤j≤m+D,−10​j≤k1,k2≤j/N0′,max⁡(j1,j2)≤10​j.m/2+N_{0}^{\prime}k_{++}+D^{2}\leq j\leq m+D,\quad-10j\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq j/N_{0}^{\prime},\quad\max(j_{1},j_{2})\leq 10j.

In this case, we may simply use (D.41) to conclude that

‖Pk​T~mσ;μ,ν​[fk1,j1μ,fk2,j2ν;Pk3​h]‖L2≲2−(1+2​β)​m​2−(N0−1)​k+⁣+\begin{split}\|P_{k}\tilde{T}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{m}[f^{\mu}_{k_{1},j_{1}},f^{\nu}_{k_{2},j_{2}};P_{k_{3}}h]\|_{L^{2}}&\lesssim 2^{-(1+2\beta)m}2^{-(N_{0}-1)k_{++}}\end{split}

and therefore

2k+⁣+​(2α​k+210​k)​2(1+β)​j​‖φ~j(k)⋅Pk​T~mσ;μ,ν​[fk1,j1μ,fk2,j2ν;Pk3​h]‖L2≲2−β​m2^{k_{++}}(2^{\alpha k}+2^{10k})2^{(1+\beta)j}\|\widetilde{\varphi}^{(k)}_{j}\cdot P_{k}\tilde{T}^{\sigma;\mu,\nu}_{m}[f^{\mu}_{k_{1},j_{1}},f^{\nu}_{k_{2},j_{2}};P_{k_{3}}h]\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 2^{-\beta m}

which suffices when combined with (D.46). ∎

Lemma D.5.

Assume that t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and that f∈C∞f\in C^{\infty} satisfies f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and

sup|x|≤1,j≤N0+3|f(j)​(x)|≤A.\sup_{|x|\leq 1,\,\,j\leq N_{0}+3}|f^{(j)}(x)|\leq A. (D.49)

Let n∈HN0n\in H^{N_{0}} be such that

‖n‖HN0+‖e−i​t​Λσ​n‖Z≤1\|n\|_{H^{N_{0}}}+\|e^{-it\Lambda_{\sigma}}n\|_{Z}\leq 1 (D.50)

for some σ∈{i,e,b}\sigma\in\{i,e,b\}. Then

supk∈ℤ(2−(1+α−β)​k+2N0​k)​‖Pk​(f⁡(n))‖L2≲A,N0∥n∥HN0+∥e−i​t​Λσn∥Z,supk∈ℤ(2−(1/2−β−α)​k+26​k)​(1+t)1+β​‖Pk​(f⁡(n))‖L∞≲A,N0∥n∥HN0+∥e−i​t​Λσn∥Z.\begin{split}\sup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}(2^{-(1+\alpha-\beta)k}+2^{N_{0}k})\|P_{k}(f(n))\|_{L^{2}}&\lesssim_{A,N_{0}}\|n\|_{H^{N_{0}}}+\|e^{-it\Lambda_{\sigma}}n\|_{Z},\\ \sup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}(2^{-(1/2-\beta-\alpha)k}+2^{6k})(1+t)^{1+\beta}\|P_{k}(f(n))\|_{L^{\infty}}&\lesssim_{A,N_{0}}\|n\|_{H^{N_{0}}}+\|e^{-it\Lambda_{\sigma}}n\|_{Z}.\end{split}
Proof.

We first assume that

‖n‖HN0+‖e−i​t​Λσ​n‖Z=1.\|n\|_{H^{N_{0}}}+\|e^{-it\Lambda_{\sigma}}n\|_{Z}=1. (D.51)

When k≥0k\geq 0, the lemma essentially follows from the following easy inequalities,

‖f⁡(u)‖HN0≲N0∥u∥HN0, and ∥∂αxf(u)∥L∞≲∑β≤α∥∂βu∥L∞.\begin{split}\|f(u)\|_{H^{N_{0}}}&\lesssim_{N_{0}}\|u\|_{H^{N_{0}}},\quad\hbox{ and }\quad\|\partial^{\alpha}_{x}f(u)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\sum_{\beta\leq\alpha}\|\partial^{\beta}u\|_{L^{\infty}}.\end{split}

This is sufficient for the first inequality; for the second, we first observe that

26​k​‖Pk​(f⁡(P≤k​n))‖L∞≲2−k​∑|α|≤7‖∂αPk​(f⁡(P≤k​n))‖L∞≲2−k​∑|α|≤7‖∂αf⁡(P≤k​n)‖L∞≲(1+s)−1−β,\begin{split}2^{6k}\|P_{k}(f(P_{\leq k}n))\|_{L^{\infty}}&\lesssim 2^{-k}\sum_{|\alpha|\leq 7}\|\partial^{\alpha}P_{k}(f(P_{\leq k}n))\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 2^{-k}\sum_{|\alpha|\leq 7}\|\partial^{\alpha}f(P_{\leq k}n)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim(1+s)^{-1-\beta},\end{split}

while using that

f⁡(n)−f⁡(P≤k​n)=∫01f′​(P≤k​n+s​P≥k+1​n)​𝑑s⋅P≥k+1​nf(n)-f(P_{\leq k}n)=\int_{0}^{1}f^{\prime}(P_{\leq k}n+sP_{\geq k+1}n)ds\cdot P_{\geq k+1}n

we see that

26​k​‖Pk​[f⁡(n)−f⁡(P≤k​n)]‖L∞≲26​k​‖P≥k+1​n‖L∞≲(1+s)−1−β2^{6k}\|P_{k}[f(n)-f(P_{\leq k}n)]\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 2^{6k}\|P_{\geq k+1}n\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim(1+s)^{-1-\beta}

which is what we wanted. If k≤0k\leq 0, since ff is smooth, we can write

f⁡(n)=C1​n+g⁡(n),C1∈ℝ,limn→0g⁡(n)n2∈ℝ.f(n)=C_{1}n+g(n),\quad C_{1}\in\mathbb{R},\,\,\lim_{n\to 0}\frac{g(n)}{n^{2}}\in\mathbb{R}.

The linear part clearly verifies the appropriate bounds by (5.17). For the nonlinear part, we use that

‖Pk​g​(n)‖L2≲23​k/2​‖g⁡(n)^‖L∞≲23​k/2​‖g⁡(n)‖L1≲23​k/2\|P_{k}g(n)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 2^{3k/2}\|\widehat{g(n)}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 2^{3k/2}\|g(n)\|_{L^{1}}\lesssim 2^{3k/2}

and

‖Pk​g​(n)‖L∞≲‖n‖L∞2≲(1+s)−2​(1+β)‖Pk​g​(n)‖L∞≲23​k​‖g⁡(n)^‖L∞≲23​k\begin{split}\|P_{k}g(n)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\lesssim\|n\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\lesssim(1+s)^{-2(1+\beta)}\\ \|P_{k}g(n)\|_{L^{\infty}}&\lesssim 2^{3k}\|\widehat{g(n)}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 2^{3k}\end{split}

and therefore, we can easily get the bounds when k≤0k\leq 0.

In the general case of (D.50), we may simply write n=δ​n~n=\delta\tilde{n} where n~\tilde{n} satisfy (D.51). Then the Lemma follow by changing f⁡(x)→δ−1​f​(δ​x)f(x)\to\delta^{-1}f(\delta x) which still satisfies (D.49). ∎
